a: the plains of Moab
p: From here to the end of Deuteronomy, Israel never moves. Everything happens on these plains.
b: The arvot Moav are the flat lands on the east bank of the Jordan, just north of the Dead Sea, facing Jericho across the river. Israel camps here from now until Joshua 3, so the rest of Numbers, all of Deuteronomy, and Moses' death all take place in one spot. Numbers 33:49 gives the camp's spread, from Beth-jeshimoth to Abel-shittim. The land had once been Moab's, but the Amorite king Sihon had taken it (21:26), and Israel had just taken it from him. That is why Balak is frightened: Israel is camped on land Moab still thinks of as its own.

a: Balak son of Zippor
p: Balak is known only from this story and later memories of it. His father's name means "bird."
b: No text outside the Bible names Balak. His father's name, Zippor, means "bird," and the rabbis noticed that the story is full of animals: a bird, a donkey, an ox, a lion, a wild ox. Joshua 24:9 says Balak "fought against Israel," by hiring a curse instead of an army, and Micah 6:5 recalls his plan. Jephthah, by contrast, notes that Balak never actually went to war with Israel (Judges 11:25). Revelation 2:14 says Balaam "taught Balak to set a trap in front of the Israelites." Note that 22:4 names him king only after Moab has already spoken, which some critics read as a sign that two forms of the story were joined.

a: the elders of Midian
p: Midian lived mainly in northwest Arabia. Here its elders stand beside Moab, which prepares for chapters 25 and 31.
b: The Midianites were tent-dwelling clans whose home was east of the Gulf of Aqaba, though they ranged widely with their camels. Moses' father-in-law Jethro was a priest of Midian (Exodus 2–3; 18), so Midian was once Israel's friend. Here Midian's elders join Moab against Israel, and in 25:6–18 a Midianite woman is at the center of the Peor crisis, leading to the war in chapter 31. Critical scholars think Midian was added to an older Moab-only story to link Balaam to Peor; many traditional readers see two allied peoples who shared grazing lands.

a: the way an ox licks the green plants of the field bare
t: An ox licking up a field
p: A farmer's picture: a herd of cattle leaves nothing green behind.
b: The image is of a grazing ox that pulls up grass with its tongue and leaves the ground bare. Moab fears that Israel's huge camp will strip the land the same way. The verb "lick up" (lachak) is used for fire licking up water in 1 Kings 18:38. It is the first of many animal images in the Balaam chapters: the donkey, the lion and the lioness (23:24; 24:9), and the wild ox (23:22; 24:8). The fearful king turns out to be right about Israel's strength, but wrong about how to stop it.

a: Balaam son of Beor
p: In 1967 archaeologists in Jordan found a wall text that names "Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods."
b: At Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan Valley, a Dutch team led by H. J. Franken found pieces of plaster with writing in red and black ink, dated to about 800 BC. Pieced together, the text begins: "The book of Balaam son of Beor, the man who was a seer of the gods." The gods come to him at night (compare 22:9, 20), and the next day he weeps and tells his people of a disaster the gods have planned. The text is in a local dialect close to Aramaic, and it shows that Balaam was a famous seer in the region, honored by a non-Israelite community east of the Jordan. It does not prove the events of Numbers, but it shows the Bible did not invent him.

a: at Pethor, which is by the River
p: "The River" in the Bible means the Euphrates. Pethor is probably Pitru, an Assyrian town on the upper Euphrates.
b: Deuteronomy 23:4 says Balaam came "from Pethor of Aram-naharaim," northern Mesopotamia. Assyrian records of Shalmaneser III (800s BC) name a town Pitru near where the Sajur River meets the Euphrates, and most scholars identify the two. That is about 400 miles from Moab, a journey of weeks, which fits Balak's two embassies. Some scholars, because the Deir Alla text was found in the Jordan Valley and because 23:7 says "from Aram," think an older story placed Balaam nearer, and some even suggest reading Aram as Edom (a one-letter difference in Hebrew). The text as it stands brings him from far away.

a: a people has come out of Egypt
p: Judith reuses Moab's fearful words, but now Israel fears an army that will lick the land clean.
b: Judith, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in the Old Testament, reuses this scene. Moab feared a crowd that would "lick clean" the land and that covered "the face of the land." In Judith the Israelites fear the Assyrians the same way: "Now these men will lick clean the face of the whole land" (Judith 7:4). Holofernes, the Assyrian general, talks like Balak. He threatens "this people that came out of Egypt" (Judith 6:5), with Moabites in his council (Judith 6:1). Achior, an Ammonite who speaks well of Israel, plays Balaam's part. Holofernes calls him "you hireling of Ammon" (Judith 6:5), as Moab hired Balaam (Deuteronomy 23:4).

a: the one you bless is blessed, and the one you curse is cursed
p: Balak claims for Balaam what God promised Abraham. The whole story will prove Balak wrong.
b: God told Abram, "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever treats you with contempt I will curse" (Genesis 12:3; compare Genesis 27:29). Balak says the same about Balaam, as if a seer controlled blessing and curse. The story answers him: Balaam can only say what God puts in his mouth (22:38), and his third poem ends by quoting God's promise back to Israel: "Blessed be everyone who blesses you, and cursed be everyone who curses you!" (24:9). In the ancient world, professional cursers were real. Egyptian "execration texts" wrote enemies' names on pots that were then smashed.

a: the fees for divination
p: The Hebrew says simply "divinations in their hands," meaning the fee or the tools for divining.
b: The word qesamim means "divinations." Most interpreters take it as the fee paid for divining, (compare the gift brought to the seer in 1 Samuel 9:7–8). Some, like Ibn Ezra, think the elders carried the tools of divination themselves. Either way, money is in the story from the start, and this is the point the New Testament fixes on: Balaam "loved the wages of wrongdoing" (2 Peter 2:15) and of false teachers, "For pay they have thrown themselves into Balaam's error" (Jude 11). The Torah forbids Israel to practice qesem (Deuteronomy 18:10–14).

a: as the LORD speaks to me
p: A foreign seer speaks of Israel's God by his personal name, YHWH.
b: Balaam, a Mesopotamian seer, calls on "the LORD," the divine name YHWH, and even says "the LORD my God" (22:18). The narrator, though, often says "God" (Elohim) came to him (22:9, 20). Scholars have long noticed this mix of names. Source critics once divided the chapter between a Yahwist and an Elohist source; others see a deliberate pattern. The theological point is plain either way: Israel's God speaks to whom he chooses, even a pagan diviner, and that diviner cannot escape him. The rabbis said God gave the nations a prophet like Moses so they could not say they had none (Numbers Rabbah 20:1).

a: Do not curse the people, because they are blessed
p: God's first word is a clear no. Why does he later say yes? Readers have answered in several ways.
b: God forbids both going and cursing. Yet in 22:20 he says "go," and in 22:22 he is angry that Balaam goes. Many traditional readers say Balaam's second request shows he wanted to go for the money, so God let him go his own way and then confronted him (Rashi; compare Psalm 81:12). Others say God's permission was real and his anger came because Balaam went eager to curse (22:32, "your way is reckless"). Critical scholars usually think the donkey episode (22:22–35) was an older, separate story in which Balaam had never received permission, and that it was later set into a story where he had.

a: Even if Balak gave me his house full of silver and gold
p: Balaam sounds like a model prophet. The New Testament and the rabbis heard greed under the words.
b: Taken at face value, this is a noble answer, and Balaam keeps his word: he never curses Israel. Some modern readers think the Numbers story itself presents Balaam well, a foreign seer forced to tell the truth. But Jewish tradition heard the opposite. Rashi notes that Balaam names a whole house full of silver and gold, which shows what he was hoping for. The Mishnah calls his disciples people with "an evil eye, a haughty spirit and a greedy soul" (Avot 5:19). The New Testament agrees: Balaam "loved the wages of wrongdoing" (2 Peter 2:15). See the chapter page for the full debate.

a: as an adversary against him
p: The Hebrew word is satan, "an adversary." Here it is God's own angel who blocks the way.
b: The phrase is le-satan lo, "as a satan to him." In the Hebrew Bible satan is an ordinary word for someone who opposes or blocks: an enemy in war (1 Kings 11:14) or an accuser in court (Psalm 109:6). In Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3 "the satan" is an accuser in God's court. Here the adversary is "the angel of the LORD" himself. Later Jewish and Christian thought developed Satan as the name of the devil, but that meaning should not be read back into this verse. The angel stands against Balaam to protect him from his own path.
orig: לְשָׂטָן לוֹ (lesatan lo), "as an adversary to him"

a: The donkey saw the angel of the LORD
t: The donkey sees, the seer does not
p: The famous seer is blind, and his donkey sees. The story is a comedy at the prophet's expense.
b: Balaam is a professional seer who claims his "eye is opened" (24:3). Yet three times his donkey sees the angel and he does not. Three times she turns aside, three times he beats her, and each time the space grows narrower: a field, a lane between walls, a spot with no room at all. Scholars point out the parallel with the three attempts to curse Israel in chapters 23–24, each from a new place. Just as the donkey cannot pass the angel, Balaam cannot get past God's word. The humor is sharp: the beast understands God better than the expert.

a: Then the LORD opened the donkey's mouth
p: Readers have taken the talking donkey as a true miracle, a vision, or a fable-like story.
b: Most Jewish and Christian readers through history took it literally: God made the donkey speak, as 2 Peter 2:16 says, "a donkey without a voice spoke with a human voice." The Mishnah lists "the mouth of the donkey" among ten things God created at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath, ready for this moment (Avot 5:6). Maimonides held that the whole episode happened in a prophetic vision (Guide 2.42). Many modern scholars read it as a folk tale, like the fables of the ancient world in which animals speak, told to mock a seer. The only other talking animal in the Bible is the serpent of Genesis 3.

a: these three times
p: The word for "times" here is regalim, literally "feet," the word later used for the three pilgrim feasts.
b: Hebrew usually says "times" with pe'amim, but here (the donkey) and in 22:32–33 (the angel) the speaker says regalim, "feet," a rare use. The rabbis noticed it and connected it with the three pilgrimage festivals (shalosh regalim) when Israel goes up "on foot" to worship (Exodus 23:14). They read the donkey as asking: do you want to curse a people that keeps three pilgrim feasts a year? (Rashi; Numbers Rabbah 20:14). It is a homily rather than the plain sense, but it shows how closely the rabbis read every word.

a: Then the LORD uncovered Balaam's eyes
p: The same verb returns in Balaam's poems, where he calls himself one "with his eyes uncovered."
b: The verb galah, "uncover, reveal," is used here when God lets Balaam see the angel. In 24:4 and 24:16 Balaam describes himself as one who "falls down with his eyes uncovered." The story makes clear where that sight came from: Balaam sees only when God opens his eyes. Compare Elisha's prayer for his servant, "open his eyes, please, and let him see" (2 Kings 6:17), and the two disciples whose "eyes were opened" at Emmaus (Luke 24:31).

a: you are rushing down a wrong road in front of me
p: The verb yarat appears only here and in Job 16:11. Its meaning is uncertain.
b: The Hebrew ki yarat ha-derekh le-negdi is hard. The verb yarat occurs elsewhere only in Job 16:11, where it seems to mean "throw" or "thrust" ("he throws me into the hands of the wicked"). Translators have guessed: "perverse" (KJV, BSB), "headlong," "reckless," "evil." The Greek translation has "your way was not pleasing." Some scholars suggest Balaam's way was "precipitous," rushing ahead. The general sense is clear: the angel blocks him because he is going the wrong way, or in the wrong spirit.

a: I have sinned
p: Balaam confesses and offers to turn back. Some read this as sincere, others as words only.
b: Balaam's "I have sinned" uses the same words as Pharaoh (Exodus 9:27), Saul (1 Samuel 15:24) and David (2 Samuel 12:13). Some interpreters see a real moment of humility. Others notice that he excuses himself at once ("I did not know") and offers to go back only "if it is wrong in your eyes," as if it were still an open question. The angel sends him on with the same order as before (22:20, 35): he will go, but he will say only God's word. The story is less about Balaam's heart than about God's control of his mouth.

a: The word God puts in my mouth
p: This phrase describes the true prophet in Deuteronomy 18:18 and Jeremiah 1:9.
b: God promises to raise up a prophet like Moses and "put my words in his mouth" (Deuteronomy 18:18), and he tells Jeremiah, "I have put my words in your mouth" (Jeremiah 1:9). The same phrase is used of Balaam (22:38; 23:5, 12, 16). So the story makes a foreign diviner, of all people, a model of how prophecy works: the speaker does not choose the words. Christian readers have pointed to Caiaphas, who prophesied without meaning to (John 11:49–52), as a similar case of God speaking through an unwilling mouth.

a: Bamoth-baal
p: The name means "high places of Baal." It was a hilltop shrine overlooking the plains.
b: Bamoth-baal (also mentioned in 21:19–20 as Bamoth, and in Joshua 13:17) was a height on the Moabite plateau, probably near Mount Nebo. A bamah was a raised place of worship, and Baal was the great storm god of Canaan. Balak takes Balaam to a series of high places, each with a view of Israel's camp: Bamoth-baal, Pisgah (23:14), and Peor (23:28). In ancient practice a curser needed to see his target. Each new place gives a better view, and each produces a stronger blessing.

a: Build me seven altars here
t: Seven altars, seven bulls, seven rams
p: Balaam begins with a lavish sacrifice. Seven was the number of completeness across the ancient Near East.
b: Fourteen animals on seven altars, repeated at each of three sites (23:14, 29), is a huge offering. Seven-fold rites appear in Mesopotamian ritual texts and at Ugarit, and in the Bible seven means fullness (Genesis 21:28–31; Job 42:8). Balaam seems to be preparing to receive an omen, possibly by watching the animals or the smoke, as Mesopotamian diviners did. The irony is that Israel's God comes to him, but not to give Balak what he paid for. The rabbis said the seven altars matched the seven altars built by the patriarchs from Abraham to Jacob (Numbers Rabbah 20:18).

a: a bare hilltop
p: The word shefi is rare. It probably means a treeless height, though some read "alone" or "quietly."
b: The Hebrew shefi occurs here and in some prophetic texts for "bare heights" (Isaiah 41:18; Jeremiah 3:2). Most translations follow that. The Greek translation took it as "straight" and the Targum as "alone, quietly." Rashi said it meant Balaam went off by himself in silence. A bare place would suit a diviner looking for omens in the sky or the flight of birds.

a: took up his poem
p: The word mashal means a proverb, a taunt or a poem in parallel lines. It is the word for all of Balaam's oracles.
b: Each speech starts "he took up his mashal" (23:7, 18; 24:3, 15, 20, 21, 23). A mashal can be a wise saying (Proverbs 1:1), a taunt song (Isaiah 14:4), or, as here, a formal poem with paired lines. The KJV's "parable" can mislead, since these are not stories. The Balaam poems are among the oldest Hebrew poetry, with old spellings and rare words, and many scholars date them earlier than the prose around them (Albright dated them to the 1100s BC). Their language is full of parallel pairs: Jacob and Israel, curse and denounce, see and watch.

a: From Aram Balak has led me
t: From Aram and the eastern mountains
p: Aram is the land of the Arameans in Syria and northern Mesopotamia, the homeland of Abraham's family.
b: Aram was the region of Haran and the upper Euphrates, where Laban lived and Jacob found his wives (Genesis 28–31). "The mountains of the east" is a poetic parallel for the same far country. Deuteronomy 23:4 places Balaam in Aram-naharaim, "Aram of the two rivers." Some scholars note that the Deir Alla inscription was found near the Jordan and suggest the poem originally said Edom, but no manuscript reads that here. See 22:5.

a: Here is a people that settles by itself
p: This line became a famous description of the Jewish people's distinct life among the nations.
b: Balaam sees Israel camped apart and calls it a people that "does not count itself one of the nations." In context it is a blessing: Israel is set apart by God, like the "private treasure" of Exodus 19:5. Deuteronomy 33:28 says Israel "dwells secure, alone." Jewish thinkers have used the verse for centuries to describe the mystery of a people that kept its identity in exile, sometimes as pride, sometimes as a lament over isolation. Rashi read it as a promise that when Israel rejoices, no other nation shares it, and when other nations are punished, Israel survives. It has also been used in modern political debate, which is a later use of an ancient blessing.

a: Who can count the dust of Jacob
p: Balaam echoes God's promise to Abraham and Jacob that their offspring would be like the dust of the earth.
b: God promised Abram, "I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth" (Genesis 13:16), and repeated it to Jacob (Genesis 28:14). Balaam, standing over Israel's huge camp, sees the promise kept. The question "who can count" is ironic in a book called Numbers that has just counted Israel twice (chapters 1 and 26). The Greek translation reads "who has calculated the seed of Jacob" (see the variant).

a: or number a fourth part of Israel
p: The Hebrew rova usually means "a quarter." Some scholars read it as "dust" from a related ancient word.
b: The traditional reading is "the fourth part," taken by the rabbis to mean one of the four sides of the camp (Numbers 2), or even its smallest part. Since the first line says "dust," several scholars suggest a word meaning "dust cloud," related to an Akkadian word, to keep the parallel. Others repoint the word as rivevot, "myriads." The Greek translation has "the families of Israel." No reading changes the main point: Israel is too many to count.

a: May I die the way the upright die
p: Balaam wishes he could share Israel's blessed end. He will in fact die by the sword (31:8).
b: The "upright" (yesharim) are Israel; the word may play on Jeshurun, a poetic name for Israel (Deuteronomy 32:15). Balaam's wish to share their end became famous because of what happened: he was killed in the Midian war (31:8; Joshua 13:22). Jewish tradition read it as a sign that he knew the truth but would not live by it. Some Christian readers took the line as a longing for life after death, though most scholars think it means a peaceful death at a good old age with descendants, as with the patriarchs (Genesis 25:8).

a: the Field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah
p: Zophim means "watchers." Pisgah is the ridge from which Moses will later see the land.
b: "Field of the Watchers" may have been a lookout point, or a place where diviners watched for omens. Pisgah is a ridge of the Abarim range near Mount Nebo, overlooking the Jordan Valley and the Dead Sea. Moses will stand there to see the promised land before he dies (Deuteronomy 3:27; 34:1). The same mountain where Balaam tried to curse Israel becomes the place where Moses sees Israel's future.

a: God is not a man, that he should lie
t: God does not change his mind
p: One of the Bible's strongest statements that God keeps his word. Compare 1 Samuel 15:29.
b: The verse is quoted almost word for word in 1 Samuel 15:29: Israel's Glory "will not lie or change his mind, for he is not a man." Yet the Bible also says God "relented" (Exodus 32:14; Jonah 3:10). Interpreters have long weighed these together. Many Jewish and Christian theologians say God's character and promises never change, while his response to people's repentance can. Here the point is that the blessing on Israel is fixed: Balak cannot buy a new word from God by changing the place of sacrifice. Hebrews 6:18 says "it is impossible for God to lie."
r: 1 Samuel 15:29; Exodus 32:14; Jonah 3:10; Malachi 3:6; Hebrews 6:17–18; Titus 1:2

a: He sees no trouble in Jacob
p: The Hebrew words aven and amal can mean moral wrong or simply trouble and disaster.
b: The KJV reads "He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob," and Christian preachers have often read it as God not counting Israel's sin against them. But aven also means misfortune or sorcery, and amal means trouble or hardship. Many modern scholars read: God sees no disaster coming for Jacob, which fits the context of a curse that cannot work. The Targum read it as "I have seen no idol-worshipers in the house of Jacob." The verse sits just before Israel's worst idolatry (25:1–3), which makes the traditional moral reading pointed.

a: a king's battle cry rings out among them
p: The teru'ah was a war shout or trumpet blast. The king is most likely God himself.
b: Teru'at melekh is the acclaim of a king, like the shout at a coronation (1 Samuel 10:24) or a battle cry. In context the king is the LORD, who "is with him." Later Jewish liturgy took this line into the Rosh Hashanah service, where the shofar is blown to proclaim God as king (compare 29:1, "a day of loud blasts"). Some critics hear an early reference to Israel's human kingship, like 24:7, but the parallel line points to God.

a: he has the horns of a wild ox
p: The KJV's "unicorn" comes from the Greek. The Hebrew re'em is the wild ox, the aurochs.
b: The re'em was the aurochs, a huge wild ox known from Assyrian hunting reliefs and hunted to extinction in the region. The Greek translators, perhaps not knowing the animal, wrote monokeros, "one-horned," and the KJV followed with "unicorn." That gave rise to many sermons on the unicorn as a symbol of Christ. The word to'aphot, here "horns," is rare; it may mean "peaks," "strength" or "horns." The image is of overwhelming power. The same line returns in 24:8.

a: For no omen works against Jacob
p: The Hebrew preposition can mean "in Israel" (no sorcery is practiced there) or "against Israel" (no spell works on it).
b: The KJV reads "there is no enchantment against Jacob," and many modern versions agree. The Hebrew be- usually means "in," and some interpreters read: Israel has no need of omens, because God tells it what he is doing. Both senses suit the story: Balaam's divining cannot touch Israel, and Israel itself is forbidden to practice divination (Deuteronomy 18:10–15), since it has a prophet instead. The words for "omen" (nachash) and "divining" (qesem) are the two standard terms for pagan fortune-telling.

a: Look, a people rises like a lioness
p: The lion images echo Jacob's blessing of Judah (Genesis 49:9) and return in 24:9.
b: Jacob called Judah "a lion's cub" that "crouches, he lies down like a lion" (Genesis 49:9). Balaam applies the image to all Israel here and again in 24:9. In the second poem the lion rises to hunt; in the third, it lies down after the meal and no one dares to rouse it. The New Testament calls Jesus "the Lion from the tribe of Judah" (Revelation 5:5), drawing on the same line of images.

a: the top of Peor
p: Peor was a mountain with a shrine of Baal. The next chapter happens in its shadow.
b: Balak's third site is Peor, a height with a shrine to Baal-Peor (25:3). Deuteronomy says Moses was buried in a valley "opposite Beth-peor" (Deuteronomy 34:6). The choice is ominous. Balaam's curses fail on the mountain, but at its foot Israel will curse itself by worshiping the god of the place (25:1–3), and 31:16 blames Balaam for that. "The wasteland" (ha-yeshimon) is the desert land north of the Dead Sea.

a: to meet with omens
p: Until now Balaam had gone off to look for omens. This time he simply looks at Israel.
b: The word nechashim means omens or signs read by a diviner, from the same root as "no omen works against Jacob" (23:23). This verse says plainly what Balaam had been doing on the bare heights (23:3, 15): practicing divination. Now he gives it up and turns toward the wilderness where Israel is camped. The next verse says "the Spirit of God came on him," the language used for Israel's own prophets and judges. The third poem is the first that comes without sacrifice or omen.

a: the Spirit of God came on him
t: The Spirit on a foreign seer
p: The phrase is used for Saul, Othniel and other leaders of Israel. Here it rests on a non-Israelite.
b: The same words describe the Spirit coming on the seventy elders and on Saul, who then prophesy (11:25; 1 Samuel 10:10; 19:20, 23), and on judges such as Othniel (Judges 3:10). It shows that God's Spirit is not limited to Israel. Christian writers such as Origen took Balaam as proof that God can speak through anyone, and Jewish tradition counted him among the seven prophets of the nations (Bavli Bava Batra 15b). The Spirit gives him words; it does not change his character, as 31:16 shows.

a: the man whose eye sees true
p: The rare word shetum may mean "opened" or "closed." The ancient versions disagree.
b: Shetum ha-ayin appears only here and in 24:15. Targum Onqelos read it as "who sees clearly," the Greek has "who sees truly," and most modern versions say "opened." The Talmud took it the other way: Balaam was blind in one eye, "as it says, shetum ha-ayin" (Bavli Sanhedrin 105a; compare Niddah 31a). The Latin Vulgate also read "whose eye is stopped up," and Rashi gives both meanings. Some scholars divide the letters to read she-tam ha-ayin, "whose eye is perfect." The Plain English "sees true" follows the Targum and Greek. A seer whose eye is shut to the world but open to visions would also fit 24:4, "yet his eyes are uncovered."

a: what the Almighty shows
p: Balaam uses the old divine name Shaddai, found mostly in Genesis and Job, and in the Deir Alla text.
b: Shaddai, traditionally "the Almighty," is the name God used with Abraham (Genesis 17:1; Exodus 6:3). Its meaning is debated: "mountain one," "of the fields," or "breasted one" have all been proposed. Remarkably, the Deir Alla inscription about Balaam names a group of gods called shaddayin, so the word was at home in Balaam's own region. In Numbers, though, Shaddai is simply a name for Israel's God, alongside El, Elyon and YHWH. Balaam's poems use all four (24:16).

a: How good are your tents, Jacob
p: Jews still say this verse when they enter a synagogue. The words of a hired curser became a morning prayer.
b: In Hebrew it begins Mah tovu ohalekha Ya'aqov. It opens the traditional Jewish morning prayers and is said on entering a synagogue, followed by Psalm 5:7 and other verses. The rabbis asked what Balaam saw that was good: one answer is that the tents' doors did not face each other, so each family's privacy was kept (Bavli Bava Batra 60a; Rashi). Another reading takes the tents as houses of study and prayer (Bavli Sanhedrin 105b). The Talmud says that every one of Balaam's blessings turned back to curse except this one, on synagogues and study houses.

a: They stretch out like streams in the valleys
p: Nechalim usually means "valleys" or streambeds. Some read "palm groves" to match the trees in the next lines.
b: The verse lists four images: nechalim, gardens by a river, aloes, cedars. Because the last two are trees, some scholars and the BSB read "palm groves," from a possible Arabic cognate. The common meaning is "wadis," valleys with seasonal streams. "Aloes" (ahalim) here are the eaglewood tree, prized for perfume (Psalm 45:8), but cedars do not grow "beside the waters," and the LORD "planted" aloes: the picture is ideal, like a garden of God, not a botanist's list. Compare the trees of Eden (Genesis 2:8–10).

a: His king will be higher than Agag
p: Agag was the king of Amalek killed in Saul's day (1 Samuel 15). Some scholars use this to date the poem.
b: Agag is the Amalekite king Saul spared and Samuel killed (1 Samuel 15:8–33). If the poem refers to that event, critical scholars say it was written or updated in the early monarchy, around 1000 BC. Others suggest "Agag" was a title for Amalek's kings, like Pharaoh for Egypt, and could appear earlier. Traditional readers take it as prediction. The Greek and the Samaritan text read "Gog," the end-time enemy of Ezekiel 38–39 (see the variant), which turned the verse into a prophecy of the last days. Later Haman is called "the Agagite" (Esther 3:1).

a: Water will flow from his buckets
p: In a dry land, water means life and prosperity. "Seed" can mean crops or offspring.
b: The line pictures a man carrying full buckets, with plenty to spare. "His seed will be by many waters" can mean his crops are well watered, or that his descendants will be many. The Targum Onqelos read the verse as a messianic one: "The king who will be anointed from his sons will grow great, and he will rule over many peoples." The Greek went further: "A man will come out of his seed" (see the variant). In both, a farming image has become a royal one, preparing for the star and scepter of 24:17.

a: Blessed be everyone who blesses you
p: The last line of the third poem quotes Isaac's blessing of Jacob (Genesis 27:29), and through it God's word to Abram.
b: Isaac said to Jacob, "Whoever curses you, cursed! Whoever blesses you, blessed!" (Genesis 27:29), echoing God's promise in Genesis 12:3. The first half of this verse echoes Jacob's blessing of Judah (Genesis 49:9). Balaam was hired because people believed "the one you bless is blessed" (22:6). Now he declares that Israel itself carries the blessing, so anyone who curses it, Balak included, brings a curse on himself. Balak's angry reaction in the next verse shows he understood.

a: He struck his hands together
p: Striking the hands was a gesture of rage or scorn, not applause.
b: In the Bible, clapping the hands together expresses anger (Ezekiel 21:17), contempt (Job 27:23; Lamentations 2:15) or grief. Balak has paid for curses three times and received blessings three times. He dismisses Balaam without the honor (kavod, also "wealth") he had promised (22:17, 37). Balaam's answer in 24:13 repeats his first answer to the messengers (22:18), making the scene a closing bracket.

a: in the last days
p: The Hebrew be-acharit ha-yamim can mean simply "in the future" or, in later books, the end of history.
b: The phrase occurs first in Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49:1) and later in the prophets (Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5; Daniel 10:14). Many scholars think its earliest meaning is "in days to come," with no end-time sense, as in the BSB. But by the time of the Dead Sea Scrolls and the New Testament, "the last days" meant the age of the Messiah (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2), and the oracle that follows was read that way. So the phrase itself helped turn 24:17 into a messianic text.
r: Genesis 49:1; Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5; Daniel 10:14; Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2

a: who knows what the Most High knows
p: The fourth poem adds a line to the third: Balaam knows the "knowledge of Elyon."
b: Elyon, "Most High," is the title of the God Melchizedek served (Genesis 14:18–20). Balaam's poems name God as El, Shaddai, Elyon and YHWH, all of them used in old Hebrew poetry (Deuteronomy 32:8; Psalm 91:1). The rabbis took the claim to "know the Most High's mind" as boasting, saying Balaam did not even know his own donkey's mind (Bavli Berakhot 7a). The same passage says he knew the one moment of the day when God's anger flares, which explains why he was hired to curse.

a: I see him, but not yet
p: Balaam sees a figure in the far future. Jews and Christians have read the figure as David, the Messiah, or both.
b: "Him" is not named. Most historical scholars think the oracle first pointed to King David, who conquered Moab and Edom (2 Samuel 8:2, 14), the very peoples named in 24:17–18. The Targums read it as the Messiah: Onqelos has "when a king shall arise from Jacob and the Messiah be anointed from Israel." Christians from Justin Martyr on have read it of Christ. Many Jewish and Christian readers hold both: David first, then the greater son of David. The words "not yet" and "not close by" made the oracle open to the future.

a: A star will march out of Jacob
p: This line was quoted by the Dead Sea Scrolls, gave Bar Kokhba his name, and lies behind the Magi's star.
b: The verb darakh means to tread or march; a star in ancient royal language stood for a king or a god. The Dead Sea Scrolls quote the verse three times: the Damascus Document reads the star as "the Interpreter of the Law" and the scepter as "the Prince of the whole community" (CD 7:18–21); 4QTestimonia lists it with other messianic texts; the War Scroll applies it to God's victory. About AD 132, Rabbi Akiva called the rebel leader Simon ben Kosiba "Bar Kokhba," "son of the star," citing this verse, and Rabbi Yohanan ben Torta answered, "Akiva, grass will grow from your jaws, and the son of David will still not have come" (Jerusalem Talmud Taanit 4:5, 68d). Matthew 2:2 tells of Magi who saw "his star," and many Christian writers linked it with Balaam, a seer from the east like them (Origen, Against Celsus 1.59–60).

a: a scepter will rise from Israel
p: The scepter echoes Jacob's blessing of Judah: "The scepter will not leave Judah" (Genesis 49:10).
b: Shevet means a ruler's rod or scepter, and also "tribe." Parallel to the star, it means a king. Genesis 49:10 uses the same word for Judah's royal line, and the two passages were read together in Jewish and Christian messianic thought. The Greek translation turned the scepter into a person: "a man will rise from Israel" (see the variant). Psalm 45:6 and Hebrews 1:8 speak of the scepter of the divine king.

a: the brows of Moab
p: Pe'atei Moav means the "corners" of Moab: the sides of the head, or the borders of the land.
b: Pe'ah is a corner or edge, used of the corners of a field (Leviticus 19:9) and of the side of the head (Leviticus 19:27). Read as "temples" or "brows," the picture is of a warrior smashing an enemy's skull. Read as "borders," it means Moab's whole territory. Jeremiah 48:45 reuses this line about Moab, with "the crown of the head" (qodqod) in the second half. The poem predicts that the king Balak fears will in fact strike Moab.

a: all the sons of Sheth
t: Who are the sons of Sheth?
p: Either Seth, Adam's son, meaning all humanity, or the Shutu, a nomad people named in Egyptian texts.
b: The Targum Onqelos read Sheth as Seth (Genesis 4:25) and translated "all the sons of men," making the star a world ruler. Many modern scholars point to the Shutu (Sutu), semi-nomads east of the Jordan named in Egyptian execration texts and in the Amarna letters, which would give a neat parallel with Moab. Jeremiah 48:45 has "sons of tumult" (sha'on), which may be a reinterpretation. The verb "tear down" (qarqar) is also uncertain, and the Samaritan text reads "the skull of" instead (see the variant).

a: Edom will become his property
p: Seir is the mountain land of Edom, south of the Dead Sea. David conquered it (2 Samuel 8:14).
b: Edom had refused Israel passage (20:14–21). The poem promises that it will become Israel's possession. David put garrisons in Edom (2 Samuel 8:14), and Edom later broke free (2 Kings 8:20–22). Jews of the Roman period, and later the rabbis, used "Edom" as a code name for Rome, so this line too was read as a promise of victory over Rome, often together with 24:24. Obadiah and Amos 9:12 continue the theme.

a: the survivors from the city
p: "The city" is not named. Many scholars read the name Ar, Moab's city, or link the line with Edom in 24:18.
b: The Hebrew me-ir means "from a city." With no city named, the line is hard. Some scholars repoint it to read Ar, the Moabite city of 21:15 and 21:28, which would tie the line back to Moab in 24:17. Others take "city" with the previous verse and read it of Edom's stronghold. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan names the city as Constantinople, reading the line as a victory over Rome's empire. The Plain English keeps the plain Hebrew.

a: Amalek was first among the nations
p: Amalek was "first" either in age, in rank, or as the first nation to attack Israel (Exodus 17).
b: Rashi and Ibn Ezra took "first" to mean that Amalek was the first nation to make war on Israel after the exodus (Exodus 17:8–16). Others read it as a boast of rank or antiquity. The poem's end, "his end will be destruction," matches God's vow to wipe out Amalek's memory (Exodus 17:14; Deuteronomy 25:17–19) and Saul's war in 1 Samuel 15. On the moral problem of that vow, see the topic page.

a: your nest is set in the rock
p: "Nest" in Hebrew is qen, a pun on Kain, the Kenites' ancestor. "Rock" may hint at Sela in Edom.
b: The Kenites were a clan linked with Moses' in-laws (Judges 1:16; 4:11) and with metalworking; their name may mean "smith." The poem plays on qen, "nest," and Qayin, Kain, in 24:22. "Rock" is sela, possibly the Edomite stronghold of that name. The nest on the cliff is a picture of safety (compare Obadiah 1:3–4; Jeremiah 49:16), but the next line says even that will not save them.

a: How long until Asshur takes you captive?
p: Asshur is usually Assyria. It may also be a desert tribe of the same name (Genesis 25:3).
b: Assyria rose to dominate the region from the 800s to the 600s BC and carried many peoples into exile, including northern Israel (2 Kings 17:6). Some scholars think the Asshurim, an Arabian tribe descended from Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:3; compare Psalm 83:8), fit better among desert peoples like the Kenites. The line is obscure in Hebrew and translators differ on whether it asks a question or states a time.

a: once God has set this in place
p: Mi-sumo El is one of the hardest phrases in the poems. The words and even the division of the letters are uncertain.
b: Read as it stands, mi yichyeh mi-sumo El is "who will live, from God's setting it?" That is, who can survive when God brings this about. Rashi and most Jewish commentators read it as a lament over the wars to come. Some scholars divide the letters differently and find a place or people name, perhaps "from the north" or a name like Ishmael, to start the last oracle the way 24:20–21 start with Amalek and the Kenites. The Greek supplied "Og" (see the variant). The Plain English gives the plain sense of the Hebrew as it stands.

a: Ships will come from the coast of Kittim
p: Kittim began as Cyprus. Later Jews read it as the Greeks and then the Romans.
b: Kittim comes from Kition, a city on Cyprus (Genesis 10:4; Isaiah 23:1). By the 100s BC the name meant western invaders: 1 Maccabees 1:1 says Alexander "came out of the land of Kittim," and Daniel 11:30 says "ships of Kittim" will come against the king of the north, which the Greek translation of Daniel renders "Romans." The Dead Sea Scrolls use Kittim for Rome. The Latin Vulgate here reads "they will come in ships from Italy." So this last oracle became, for later readers, a prophecy of Rome. "Eber" may be the Hebrews or peoples "beyond" the river.
r: Genesis 10:4; Isaiah 23:1; Jeremiah 2:10; Daniel 11:30; 1 Maccabees 1:1; 1 Maccabees 8:5

a: went back to his place
p: The story says he went home. 31:8 says he was killed among the Midianites, so he must have stayed or returned.
b: The two notices puzzle readers. The rabbis said Balaam set out for home but turned back to Midian to collect his fee for the advice that led to Peor (Bavli Sanhedrin 106a; compare 31:16). Critical scholars say the Balaam of chapters 22–24, who blesses Israel and leaves, comes from a different tradition than the Balaam of chapter 31, who gives evil advice and dies. Either way, the Bible's later memory of Balaam follows chapter 31 as much as chapters 22–24.

a: Shittim
p: The name means "acacia trees." Joshua will send the spies from here (Joshua 2:1).
b: Shittim, also called Abel-shittim, "meadow of the acacias" (33:49), was Israel's last camp before crossing the Jordan. It is usually placed at Tell el-Hammam or Tell Kefrein, northeast of the Dead Sea. Joshua sends the spies to Jericho from Shittim (Joshua 2:1), and Israel sets out from there to cross the river (Joshua 3:1). Micah 6:5 asks Israel to remember "what happened from Shittim to Gilgal," linking the Balaam story and this disaster with the crossing.

a: to commit sexual sin with the daughters of Moab
p: The verb zanah means sexual immorality, and it is also the Bible's word for unfaithfulness to God.
b: Zanah is used for prostitution and sexual sin, and the prophets use it for Israel's worship of other gods, pictured as a wife's unfaithfulness (Hosea 1–3; Ezekiel 16). Here both meanings are present: sex with Moabite women leads to meals for their gods and worship (25:2). Some older scholars thought this described ritual sex in a fertility cult, but there is little clear evidence for such cults in the region, and many now doubt it. Paul warns, "We must not commit sexual sin as some of them did, and 23,000 fell in a single day" (1 Corinthians 10:8).

a: The women invited the people to the sacrifices for their gods
p: Sacrifices were usually eaten. To eat at a god's feast was to join in that god's worship.
b: In the ancient world most sacrifices ended in a shared meal, and eating meat from the altar meant fellowship with the god. Exodus 34:15–16 warns of exactly this: "someone will invite you and you will eat from his sacrifice," and then their daughters will "lead your sons to chase after their gods too." Psalm 106:28 says Israel "tied themselves to the Baal of Peor and ate the sacrifices of the dead," which may point to a feast for dead ancestors (a marzeach). Paul's warnings about food offered to idols draw on this chapter (1 Corinthians 10:7–8, 18–21).

a: tied itself to the Baal of Peor
p: The verb tsamad means to harness or fasten together, like animals under one yoke.
b: The rare verb tsamad (also in 25:5 and Psalm 106:28) is used of yoking animals or fastening a bracelet. Israel ties itself to Baal-Peor as if in a harness. Paul may echo the image when he warns believers not to be "yoked" with unbelievers in idol worship (2 Corinthians 6:14–16). Baal was the Canaanite storm and fertility god; "Baal of Peor" was his local form at the mountain shrine of Peor (23:28). Hosea 9:10 says Israel "came to Baal-peor and devoted themselves to the shameful thing."

a: impale them before the LORD in the open sun
p: The verb hoqa' is rare. It may mean impale, hang, or expose the bodies. And "them" may be the heads of the people or the guilty.
b: Hoqa' appears again only in 2 Samuel 21:6–9, where seven of Saul's descendants are executed "before the LORD" and their bodies left exposed. Translations range from "hang" (KJV) to "impale" or "execute." The Greek has "make an example of them." A second question: are the chiefs themselves to die, or are they to execute the guilty? Rashi and the Targums say the chiefs were to judge and execute the guilty, which fits 25:5. Some modern scholars read it as the chiefs being held responsible. The Samaritan text appears to remove the problem (see the variant).

a: an Israelite man came, bringing a Midianite woman
p: The man brings the woman openly into the camp while the people mourn at the sanctuary.
b: The timing is the point: Israel is weeping at the tent of meeting over the plague (which is mentioned only in 25:8–9), and this man walks past with a Midianite woman "right before the eyes of Moses." Ancient and modern readers have taken this as a deliberate defiance. Josephus gives Zimri a long speech defending his freedom against Moses' "tyranny" (Antiquities 4.145–149). The Talmud imagines him asking Moses, "Is this one forbidden? Then who allowed you Jethro's daughter?" (Bavli Sanhedrin 82a), since Moses' own wife was Midianite.

a: the inner tent
p: The rare word qubbah means a domed tent or alcove. It is a pun with "her belly" (qevatah).
b: Qubbah appears only here. It may be a curved tent, a sleeping alcove, or a shrine tent (some have compared the Arabic qubbah, a domed shrine, and the portable red-leather tents of pre-Islamic Arab tribes). If it was a shrine, the act may have been a ritual. The spear passes "through her belly" (qevatah), a sound-play with qubbah. The Talmud reads the detail as proof that Phinehas caught them in the act (Bavli Sanhedrin 82b).

a: twenty-four thousand
p: Paul says 23,000 fell "in a single day." Readers have long tried to reconcile the two numbers.
b: 1 Corinthians 10:8 says "23,000 fell in a single day." All Hebrew and Greek manuscripts of Numbers read 24,000. Explanations: Paul is giving round numbers; Paul counts only those who died in one day, while Numbers counts the full plague including the executions of 25:5; or Paul is thinking of a figure from memory, perhaps blending with the 3,000 of Exodus 32:28. Many scholars simply call it a slip of memory or a rounded figure. The point in both texts is the same.

a: was zealous with my zeal among them
p: The same Hebrew word means jealousy and zeal. God is "jealous" for Israel as a husband for his wife.
b: Qana and qin'ah are used of God's jealousy in the Ten Words (Exodus 20:5; 34:14, "the LORD, whose name is Jealous"), and of a husband's jealousy (5:14). In this chapter Israel has been unfaithful to God, and Phinehas shares God's own passion. The word appears four times in 25:11–13. It became the root of the name "Zealots," the Jewish movement against Rome in the first century AD, who looked to Phinehas as their model. Paul says that before his conversion he was "extremely zealous" (Galatians 1:14).

a: my covenant: peace
p: God gives Phinehas "my covenant: peace." In the scroll, the letter vav of "peace" is written broken.
b: Beriti shalom can be read "my covenant of peace" or "my covenant, namely peace." Isaiah 54:10 and Ezekiel 34:25; 37:26 speak of a future "covenant of peace." Malachi 2:4–6 recalls God's covenant with Levi as "life and peace." In Torah scrolls the letter vav in shalom is traditionally written with a break in it (vav qetiah). Bavli Kiddushin 66b uses the broken letter to teach that a priest with a blemish is not "whole" (shalem) and may not serve. Later preachers read it as a sign that peace won through violence is never whole, and others said Phinehas' covenant stood complete in spite of the broken letter.

a: a covenant of priesthood for all time
p: The high priests of Solomon's temple, the Zadokites, traced their line to Phinehas.
b: Phinehas became high priest after Eleazar (Judges 20:28). 1 Chronicles 6:4–8 traces Zadok, Solomon's high priest, to Eleazar and Phinehas, and Ezekiel 44:15 gives the Zadokites alone the right to serve at the altar. Ben Sira praises Phinehas as "third in glory" after Moses and Aaron (Sirach 45:23–24). Mattathias, the priest who began the Maccabean revolt, "was zealous for the law, as Phinehas had been against Zimri son of Salu" (1 Maccabees 2:26). Dying, he told his sons that Phinehas "received the covenant of a holy priesthood" (1 Maccabees 2:54). The "perpetual" priesthood was interrupted when the temple fell in AD 70, a problem that later Jewish and Christian writers both took up.
r: Judges 20:28; 1 Chronicles 6:4–8; Ezekiel 44:15; Sirach 45:23–24; 1 Maccabees 2:26; 1 Maccabees 2:54; Hebrews 7:11–17

a: made atonement for the Israelites
p: The text says Phinehas' act "made atonement." Readers have struggled with what that means.
b: Usually a priest makes atonement (kipper) with blood on the altar. Here an act of execution turns away God's anger, as Aaron's incense did when he stood between the dead and the living (16:46–48). Psalm 106:30–31 says, "But Phinehas rose and gave judgment, and the plague was held back. It was reckoned to him as righteousness," the words Genesis 15:6 uses of Abram's trust. Jewish law limited the precedent: the Mishnah allows zealots to act only in the very moment (Sanhedrin 9:6), and the Talmud says that if a zealot asked a court beforehand, they would not tell him to do it (Bavli Sanhedrin 82a). See the chapter page.

a: Zimri son of Salu
p: Zimri was a leader, not a nobody. The tribe of Simeon shrinks sharply in the next census.
b: Naming Zimri as a leader in Simeon shows the sin reached Israel's leadership, which may explain 25:4. In the first census Simeon had 59,300 men (1:23); in the second only 22,200 (26:14), the largest drop of any tribe. Many interpreters, ancient and modern, connect the two and suppose most of the plague's victims were Simeonites. Moses does not bless Simeon at all in Deuteronomy 33.

a: Cozbi daughter of Zur
p: The woman is the daughter of Zur, one of the five kings of Midian killed in 31:8.
b: Cozbi's father Zur is named among the kings of Midian in 31:8 and the princes of Sihon in Joshua 13:21. Her name may mean "voluptuous" or may play on kazav, "lie, deceit," matching God's charge that Midian dealt "with tricks" (25:18). The high rank of both people makes this an affair of state, which is how the chapter reads it: Midian used its women to draw Israel away from God, a charge 31:16 lays at Balaam's feet.

a: Treat the Midianites as enemies
p: Moab led the seduction (25:1), but Midian is the target of revenge. Several reasons have been given.
b: The command looks ahead to chapter 31. Deuteronomy 2:9 tells Israel not to attack Moab, since God gave Moab its land as Lot's descendants, which may explain why Midian bears the punishment. The rabbis said Moab acted out of fear, but Midian joined in a quarrel not its own (Rashi; Sifre). Critical scholars think two stories have been joined, a Moabite one (25:1–5) and a Midianite one (25:6–18), with the second shaped to introduce the war of chapter 31.

a: After the plague
p: The second census marks the turning point of the book: the old generation is gone, and a new one stands ready.
b: In Hebrew Bibles the words "After the plague" end chapter 25 (as 25:19); English Bibles begin chapter 26 with them. The census mirrors the one in chapter 1, almost forty years earlier, with the same order of tribes except that Manasseh comes before Ephraim. Dennis Olson argued that these two censuses are the backbone of Numbers: the death of the old generation (chapters 1–25) and the birth of the new (26–36). Every name counted here, except Caleb and Joshua, is new (26:64–65).

a: Count the heads
p: The Hebrew idiom for taking a census is "lift up the head." The same phrase can mean to honor someone.
b: Se'u et-rosh, "lift the head," is the census idiom (1:2; Exodus 30:12). In Genesis 40:13, 20 Joseph plays on the double sense: Pharaoh will "lift up the head" of the cupbearer to restore him, and of the baker to hang him. The census counts men "who can go out to war," so its purpose is military: Israel is about to fight for the land. It also decides the size of each tribe's inheritance (26:52–56).

p: The total, 601,730 men of fighting age, suggests about two million people. Many scholars find that impossible.
b: Read as "thousands," the totals imply a population of two to three million in the desert, far more than Egypt's whole army and more than the Sinai could feed. Traditional readers accept the figures as miracle. Others note that Hebrew elef can mean a "clan" or a military "unit" (Judges 6:15), so "43 units, 730 men" would give much smaller numbers (Mendenhall; Humphreys). Critical scholars usually think the lists are idealized, perhaps reflecting the population of a later period.

a: These are the same Dathan and Abiram
p: The census pauses to recall the rebellion of chapter 16.
b: Dathan and Abiram, Reubenites, joined Korah in challenging Moses (16:1–35). The census stops to remember their fate, perhaps because they belonged to Reuben, Israel's firstborn, whose leadership claim they may have pressed. Psalm 106:16–18 and Deuteronomy 11:6 also recall it. The phrase "men called from the community" matches 16:2. Jude 11 names "Korah's revolt" among the warnings to the church.

a: But the sons of Korah did not die
p: Korah's family line survived. Its descendants became temple singers who wrote eleven psalms.
b: Chapter 16 might suggest Korah's whole household died (16:32). This verse says his sons lived. The rabbis said they repented in time and a ledge was made for them in the pit (Bavli Sanhedrin 110a; Rashi). Their descendants became gatekeepers and singers in the temple (1 Chronicles 6:22–37; 9:19), and Psalms 42, 44–49, 84–85 and 87–88 are titled "of the sons of Korah." By Chronicles' account the prophet Samuel came from this line too (1 Chronicles 6:33–38).

p: Simeon falls from 59,300 to 22,200, the largest loss of any tribe.
b: Compare 1:23. Five tribes shrink and seven grow, and the total is almost the same: 603,550 in the first census (1:46) and 601,730 now. Simeon's drop is often linked to the plague at Peor, where the Simeonite chief Zimri was killed (25:14). In Joshua 19:1–9 Simeon receives only towns inside Judah's land, and the tribe later seems to have been absorbed into Judah.

a: Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan
p: The census remembers the story of Judah and Tamar in Genesis 38.
b: Er and Onan both died for their wickedness (Genesis 38:7–10), and Judah's line continued through Shelah and through Perez and Zerah, the twins born to Tamar (Genesis 38:27–30). Perez is the ancestor of David (Ruth 4:18–22) and appears in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3). Judah is again the largest tribe, as in chapter 1.

a: Iezer, the clan of the Iezerites
t: Manasseh's clans in the Samaria ostraca
p: Several of these clan names turn up as district names on pottery records from Samaria, about 780 BC.
b: The Samaria ostraca are pieces of pottery with ink notes recording deliveries of wine and oil to the royal city of Samaria in the 700s BC. They name districts including Abiezer (Iezer), Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Shemida, and two of Zelophehad's daughters: Hoglah and Noah (26:33). Joshua 17:2–3 also lists these clans. So the names of Manasseh's clans and "daughters" were real places in the hill country of Samaria. Scholars debate whether the census borrowed geography or the districts were named after the clans.

a: Zelophehad son of Hepher had no sons, only daughters
p: Women are rarely named in census lists. These five are named because their case is coming (27:1–11).
b: The census lists men, but it stops to name Zelophehad's five daughters. Their names come up again in 27:1, 36:11, Joshua 17:3 and 1 Chronicles 7:15. Naming them in the census sets up the legal question of the next chapter: if a man has no sons, does his family's name and land disappear? The land will be divided by the names counted here (26:53), which is why they press their claim.

a: The name of Asher's daughter was Serah
p: Serah is named in Genesis 46:17 among those who went to Egypt. Jewish legend says she lived for centuries.
b: Serah is one of very few women named in the genealogies (Genesis 46:17; 1 Chronicles 7:30). Because she appears both in the list of those who went down to Egypt and in this census of the exodus generation's children, the rabbis told stories that she lived through the whole period. The Talmud says she showed Moses where Joseph's coffin lay (Bavli Sotah 13a); later midrash says she told Jacob that Joseph was alive by singing to him, and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 46:17 says she was taken into the Garden of Eden alive. Most scholars read her as the name of a clan.

p: The new total is 1,820 less than forty years earlier. A generation died, but Israel held its numbers.
b: The first census gave 603,550 (1:46). After forty years of wilderness, the deaths at Kibroth-hattaavah, after the spies, in Korah's revolt and at Peor, the people are almost exactly as many as before. Readers have taken this as a sign that God kept his promise to Abraham even while judging the rebels. On the size of the numbers, see the note at 26:7.

a: A big group gets a big inheritance
p: The land is divided by size (26:54) and also by lot (26:55). How do the two fit?
b: Rabbinic tradition combined them: the lot chose each tribe's region, and the size of the region was set by the tribe's numbers (Rashi; Bavli Bava Batra 122a). The Talmud says the lot was drawn under the Holy Spirit, with Eleazar wearing the Urim, so the lot itself called out the tribe's name. Some critical scholars see two different systems that were combined. Joshua 14–19 describes the casting of lots at Shiloh.

a: Jochebed, daughter of Levi
p: Moses' mother is named here and in Exodus 6:20. Her name may contain the divine name: "YHWH is glory."
b: Exodus 2 does not name Moses' parents; Exodus 6:20 says Amram married his aunt Jochebed, a marriage later forbidden (Leviticus 18:12). Her name, Yokheved, may begin with a short form of YHWH, which is striking if the name was first revealed to Moses (Exodus 6:3). The verse adds that she was "born to Levi in Egypt," which would make her very old at Moses' birth if Levi's own daughter is meant; many take "daughter of Levi" to mean a Levite woman. Miriam is named as Aaron and Moses' sister.

a: a month old and up
p: Levites were counted from one month old, not twenty, because they were not soldiers but God's own.
b: The Levites were counted separately in chapter 3, from a month old (3:15, 39), as a ransom in place of Israel's firstborn. Their total grows from 22,000 (3:39) to 23,000. They do not receive a tribal territory, because "the LORD is their inheritance" (18:20, 24); instead they will receive towns among the other tribes (35:1–8).

a: except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun
p: God swore that the exodus generation would die in the wilderness (14:29). The census proves it done.
b: In 14:28–35 God said that every man counted from twenty years old would fall in the wilderness except Caleb and Joshua. This census shows the oath fulfilled: no one counted in chapter 1 remains. Hebrews 3:16–19 asks, "With whom was he angry for forty years? Wasn't it with those who sinned, whose dead bodies lay fallen in the wilderness?" It draws the lesson of unbelief. Eleazar has replaced Aaron, and a new generation stands at the Jordan.

a: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah
p: Several of the sisters' names are also place names in the hill country of Manasseh.
b: Tirzah was a city that later served as the capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 14:17; 16:23), and Hoglah and Noah appear as districts in the Samaria ostraca (see 26:30). Many scholars think the story explains how certain towns or clans came to belong to Manasseh through "daughter" lines. Jewish tradition reads them as real women and praises them highly: "The daughters of Zelophehad were wise, they were interpreters of Scripture, they were righteous" (Bavli Bava Batra 119b). Their order changes in 36:11, which the Talmud explains: they were listed by wisdom in one place and by age in the other.

a: at the entrance of the tent of meeting
p: The sisters stand before Moses, the high priest, the leaders and the whole community: the highest court in Israel.
b: The entrance of the tent was the place of public judgment (compare 16:18–19). For five unmarried women to bring a legal claim before that whole assembly was bold. The Talmud gives two opinions on the order of the verse: one says they came first to the lower leaders, who sent them up the line until they reached Moses; the other reverses the order (Bavli Bava Batra 119b; Rashi follows the first). Modern readers, including feminist scholars, have praised their courage, while also pointing out that the law they won still worked inside a system built around men's names and men's land (see 36:1–12).

a: It was for his own sin that he died
p: The daughters say their father was not one of Korah's rebels. He died, like the rest of his generation, for his own sin.
b: Their point is legal: Korah's followers may have lost their property rights, but their father did not rebel and should not lose his name. "His own sin" probably means only that he died with his generation in the wilderness (14:29–35). The Talmud records a debate: Rabbi Akiva identified Zelophehad with the man stoned for gathering wood on the Sabbath (15:32–36), while Rabbi Judah ben Bathyra rebuked him for naming a sinner the Torah left unnamed (Bavli Shabbat 96b–97a). Others guessed he was among those who tried to go up to Canaan after God forbade it (14:40–45).

a: Why should our father's name disappear from his clan
p: In ancient Israel the family's land carried the family's name. Without an heir, both would vanish.
b: A man's "name" lived on in his land and his descendants. That is why the levirate law of Deuteronomy 25:5–10 has a brother produce an heir "so that his name will not be wiped out from Israel," and why Boaz redeems Elimelech's field "to raise up the dead man's name on his inheritance" (Ruth 4:5, 10). The daughters ask for a different answer: let us carry our father's name through the land. Ancient Near Eastern documents from Nuzi, Emar and elsewhere show that daughters could inherit when there were no sons, sometimes by being legally made "sons."

a: So Moses brought their case before the LORD
t: A case Moses could not answer
p: Moses does not know the answer and asks God. The rabbis saw a lesson in his humility.
b: This is one of four cases in the Torah where Moses has to ask God for a ruling: the man who cursed God's name (Leviticus 24:10–16), those unclean at Passover (9:6–14), the Sabbath wood-gatherer (15:32–36), and this one. The rabbis said Moses had to ask because he had once said, "Bring me any case that is too hard for you, and I will hear it" (Deuteronomy 1:17), and so he learned humility (Sanhedrin 8a; Rashi). Modern readers note that the law here grows through a real case, as laws do, rather than coming down all at once.

a: Zelophehad's daughters have spoken rightly
p: God's answer is not just a ruling. He says the women are right.
b: Ken benot Tselofchad dovrot: "Rightly the daughters of Zelophehad speak." Rashi says God declared that their reading matched what was written before him on high, and that they saw what Moses had not. The Sifre says, "Happy is the person whose words God agrees with." The verb in "you must give" is strengthened (naton titten), and the pronoun "to them" is masculine (lahem), which the rabbis noticed (Bavli Bava Batra 118b–119a). Jewish law built its whole order of inheritance on 27:8–11 (Mishnah Bava Batra 8:1–2).
orig: כֵּן בְּנוֹת צְלָפְחָד דֹּבְרֹת (ken benot tselofchad doverot)

a: When a man dies without a son
p: The new law puts daughters first after sons. It is a gain for women, and also a limited one.
b: The order is: sons, then daughters, then brothers, father's brothers, and the nearest relative. A wife does not inherit from her husband, and daughters inherit only when there are no sons. Rabbinic law kept this order but provided for daughters' support and dowries from the estate (Mishnah Ketubot 4:6; Bava Batra 9:1). Interpreters differ on how to judge it. Many see real progress for its time, since daughters are recognized as heirs. Others, including many feminist readers, stress that the law protects the father's name and land rather than the women themselves, as 36:1–12 shows.

a: a rule of law
p: The phrase marks a lasting legal ruling. It returns in 35:29 for the law of the cities of refuge.
b: Chuqqat mishpat joins the two main words for law: choq, a fixed rule, and mishpat, a judgment or ruling. It appears only here and in 35:29. The ruling given for one family becomes binding "for the Israelites," a precedent for all.

a: Go up this mountain of the Abarim range
p: God tells Moses he will see the land but not enter it. The scene is carried out in Deuteronomy 34.
b: The Abarim ("regions beyond") are the mountains east of the Dead Sea, including Mount Nebo and Pisgah. The command is repeated in Deuteronomy 32:48–52 and fulfilled in Deuteronomy 34:1–5, where Moses dies after seeing the land from Nebo. The placement here, right after the daughters' case, is striking: they win a share in the land, and Moses learns he will have none.

a: you will be gathered to your people
p: An old phrase for death, used of the patriarchs. It may reflect a belief in joining one's ancestors.
b: The phrase is used of Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and Aaron (Genesis 25:8, 17; 35:29; 49:33; 20:24). It is not the same as burial, since Jacob is "gathered" before he is buried, and Moses' burial place is unknown (Deuteronomy 34:6). Many scholars think it reflects a belief that the dead join their ancestors in some form of existence. Aaron's death on Mount Hor is told in 20:22–29 and dated in 33:38.

a: you two rebelled against my word
p: God recalls the waters of Meribah (20:1–13). The reason Moses cannot enter the land is still debated.
b: In 20:12 God says Moses and Aaron "You did not believe me, to treat me as holy in the Israelites' eyes." What exactly was the sin? Interpreters have suggested: striking the rock instead of speaking to it (Rashi), Moses' anger in calling the people "rebels" (Maimonides), or saying "must we bring water" as if the miracle were theirs (Ramban, citing others). Deuteronomy 1:37 says God was angry with Moses "because of you," the people. Psalm 106:32–33 says "Moses came to harm on their account." The narrator's added note explains which waters are meant.

a: the God of the spirits of all flesh
p: Moses uses a title first heard in 16:22: God gives the breath of life to every living being.
b: In 16:22 Moses and Aaron used this title in pleading for the people. Here Moses uses it to ask God, who knows every person's spirit, to choose the next leader. Rashi says Moses meant: you know each person's temper, so appoint one who can bear with each of them. Hebrews 12:9 speaks of "the Father of spirits." Moses does not ask for his own sons to succeed him.

a: like sheep with no one to shepherd them
p: Moses' phrase returns in the prophets and in the Gospels, where Jesus pities crowds with no shepherd.
b: The "go out and come in" lines are military: a leader goes ahead in battle and brings the troops home (1 Samuel 18:16). The prophet Micaiah saw "all Israel scattered on the mountains like a flock with no shepherd" (1 Kings 22:17), and Ezekiel 34 condemns Israel's failed shepherds. Matthew 9:36 and Mark 6:34 use the words for Jesus' compassion. Christian readers note that Joshua's name in Greek is "Jesus" (Hebrews 4:8), and see in Moses' prayer a longing fulfilled in the Good Shepherd (John 10:11).
r: 1 Samuel 18:16; 1 Kings 22:17; Ezekiel 34:5; Zechariah 10:2; Matthew 9:36; Mark 6:34; John 10:11

a: a man who has the Spirit in him
p: Joshua already has the Spirit. The laying on of hands passes on Moses' authority, not the Spirit itself, in this verse.
b: Here Joshua is chosen because the Spirit is already in him. But Deuteronomy 34:9 says, "Moses had laid his hands on Joshua son of Nun, and so Joshua was filled with a spirit of wisdom." The two verses are read together in Jewish and Christian tradition. Christians see in this rite the pattern for ordination (Acts 6:6; 1 Timothy 4:14). Jewish ordination of rabbis, semikhah, "leaning" of the hands, takes its name from this verb and traces a chain back to Moses and Joshua (Mishnah Avot 1:1).

a: Put some of your honor on him
p: The word hod means majesty or splendor. Moses gives Joshua part of it, not all.
b: Hod is royal or divine splendor (Psalm 104:1; 1 Chronicles 29:25). The word "some of" (me-) caught the rabbis' attention: "some of, and not all of it." The Talmud says, "The face of Moses was like the face of the sun, the face of Joshua like the face of the moon" (Bavli Bava Batra 75a). Compare the shining of Moses' face (Exodus 34:29–35). No later leader will speak with God face to face as Moses did (12:8; Deuteronomy 34:10).

a: the decision of the Urim
p: Joshua will not hear God directly as Moses did. He will learn God's will through the priest's Urim.
b: The Urim (and Thummim) were objects kept in the high priest's breastpiece and used to receive yes-or-no answers from God (Exodus 28:30; 1 Samuel 14:41). Moses spoke with God "mouth to mouth" (12:8), but Joshua must stand before Eleazar to ask. So leadership is now divided between a military leader and a priest, a pattern that continues in Israel's later history. The Urim are mentioned for the last time in Ezra 2:63 and Nehemiah 7:65, as lost.

a: He laid his hands on him
p: God told Moses to lay his hand (singular) on Joshua. Moses laid both hands.
b: In 27:18 the Hebrew has "your hand"; here Moses lays "his hands." Rashi says Moses did more than he was told, generously, "like a full and overflowing vessel." The Samaritan Pentateuch and the scroll 4QNum-b add words from Deuteronomy 3:21–22 at this point (see the variant).

a: It is my food
p: The offerings are called God's "food" (lechem). Israel did not think God was hungry, but the old word stayed.
b: Lachmi, "my bread, my food," is an old word for sacrifices (Leviticus 3:11; 21:6). Other ancient peoples spoke of feeding their gods, and Mesopotamian temples served daily meals to statues. Israel kept the word but rejected the idea: "Suppose I were hungry: I would not say so to you" (Psalm 50:12–13). Jewish interpreters said the language is for human understanding. The offering is a gift (qorban, "what is brought near"), and its "soothing smell" pictures God's pleasure in it.

a: at its set time
p: Chapters 28–29 list the public offerings for every day, week, month and festival of the year.
b: Leviticus 23 lists the holy days; Numbers 28–29 lists what must be offered on each. The order goes from the most frequent to the rarest: daily, Sabbath, new moon, then the feasts of the first month and the seventh month. Each set is added on top of the one before, so the daily offering is never skipped. Added up, the yearly total comes to 113 bulls and 1,093 lambs, besides rams and goats. Why place this calendar here? Many think it is a charge to the new generation about to enter the land, where such offerings would become possible.

a: as a regular burnt offering
p: The word tamid, "regular, continual," became the name of the daily offering.
b: Olat tamid, the "regular burnt offering," was offered every morning and evening (Exodus 29:38–42). The Mishnah has a whole tractate, Tamid, describing how priests carried it out in the Second Temple. Daniel 8:11–13 and 11:31 describe a king who "took away the tamid," which Jews remembered as the work of Antiochus IV in 167 BC. After the temple fell in AD 70, the morning and afternoon prayers (Shacharit and Minchah) took the place of the tamid, and this passage is read daily in many prayer books. Hebrews 10:11 contrasts priests offering "day after day" with Christ's one sacrifice.

a: between the two evenings
p: This phrase is the time of the evening offering and of the Passover lamb. Its exact meaning was debated.
b: Bein ha-arbayim is used for the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:6) and the evening tamid. The Pharisees and the Mishnah took it as the afternoon, from when the sun starts to go down until sunset, and the evening tamid was offered at about 3 p.m. (Mishnah Pesachim 5:1; Josephus). The Samaritans and Karaites took it as the time between sunset and full dark. Acts 3:1 mentions "the hour of prayer, the ninth hour," which matches the afternoon offering.

a: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour
p: A tenth of an ephah is about two quarts of flour; a quarter of a hin is about a quart of oil.
b: The ephah was a dry measure of perhaps 20 to 40 liters (estimates vary). A tenth of an ephah, also called an omer (Exodus 16:36), is roughly two quarts. The hin, a liquid measure, was about a gallon, so a quarter hin is about a quart. The scale rises with the animal: a lamb takes one tenth, a ram two, a bull three; wine rises from a quarter to a third to a half hin (28:12–14; 15:1–12). The "oil from beaten olives" was the finest grade, crushed by hand rather than pressed.

a: Pour out a drink offering of strong drink
p: Shekar usually means beer or other strong drink. Its use here surprised later interpreters.
b: Shekar is any intoxicating drink other than wine, probably beer (Leviticus 10:9 forbids priests to drink it while serving). Here it is poured out to God, and 28:14 calls the libation "wine." The rabbis said the word here means wine that intoxicates, that is, aged wine (Bavli Sukkah 49b). "In the holy place" was taken to mean poured on the altar. The drink offering was never drunk by the worshiper.

a: On the Sabbath day
p: This is the only place in the Torah that sets an extra offering for the Sabbath.
b: The Sabbath doubles the daily offering: two more lambs. It is the only Sabbath sacrifice in the Torah, though the twelve loaves of the bread of presence were also set out each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:8). Jesus noted that priests "break the Sabbath" by working in the temple and are innocent (Matthew 12:5), which refers to offerings like this. Jews call the extra service on Sabbaths and feasts Musaf, "addition," from the phrase "on top of the regular burnt offering."

a: At the beginnings of your months
p: Israel's months began with the new moon. It was a festival day with offerings and trumpet blasts.
b: Israel used a lunar calendar, and the first sliver of the new moon began each month. Trumpets were blown over the new moon offerings (10:10). The prophets mention new moons with Sabbaths as times of worship (Isaiah 1:13–14; Amos 8:5), and Paul mentions them among "a shadow of what was to come" (Colossians 2:16–17). In Judaism Rosh Chodesh is still a minor festival, especially honored by women in some traditions.

a: as a sin offering
p: The hatta't is traditionally the "sin offering." Many scholars prefer "purification offering."
b: Every festival includes one male goat as a hatta't. Jacob Milgrom argued that its purpose was to cleanse the sanctuary from the impurity caused by Israel's sins and uncleanness, so "purification offering" fits better. The traditional name is kept here, following this book's practice. The goat at the new moon is specially said to be "to the LORD," and the rabbis made a homily about God himself needing atonement for shrinking the moon (Bavli Chullin 60b), a famous piece of rabbinic storytelling.

a: is the LORD's Passover
p: Passover on the 14th and the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread from the 15th together recall the exodus.
b: The Passover lamb was killed on the afternoon of the 14th (Exodus 12:6) and eaten that night, the start of the 15th. Then came seven days of unleavened bread. This list gives only the public offerings for the seven days; the Passover lamb itself was a family offering. Israel had last kept Passover in the second year (9:1–5). The New Testament links Jesus' death with Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7; John 19:36).

a: Do no daily work
p: Melekhet avodah means ordinary labor. On festivals it is forbidden, but cooking is allowed.
b: The Sabbath and the Day of Atonement forbid "all work" (29:7). The other feast days forbid melekhet avodah, literally "work of service," that is, one's regular daily work. Exodus 12:16 allows food to be prepared on festivals, and Jewish law has kept that difference: one may cook on a festival day but not on the Sabbath (Mishnah Megillah 1:5).

a: the day of the first fruits
p: The Feast of Weeks comes fifty days after Passover. Christians know it as Pentecost.
b: Leviticus 23:15–21 sets the date: count seven weeks from the waving of the first sheaf. Here it is called "the day of the first fruits," the wheat harvest. Its Greek name, Pentecost, means "fiftieth." Later Judaism linked it with the giving of the law at Sinai, which came in the third month (Exodus 19:1). In Acts 2 the Spirit is poured out on this feast. The offering list here differs slightly from Leviticus 23:18 (two bulls and one ram here, one bull and two rams there); the rabbis said the two lists are separate sets offered together (Menachot 45b).

a: It will be a day of loud blasts for you
p: The Torah calls it "a day of loud blasts." Later Judaism made it the New Year, Rosh Hashanah.
b: Yom teru'ah means a day of shouting or trumpet blasts. The Torah does not call it a new year; the year's first month was in spring (Exodus 12:2). But the seventh month began the agricultural year in the fall, and by the time of the Mishnah the first of Tishri was Rosh Hashanah, "head of the year," a day of judgment when the shofar (ram's horn) is blown (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1; 4:9). Christians have sometimes linked the day with the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15:52, a connection the text itself does not make.

a: These are on top of the burnt offering of the new moon
p: The first of the seventh month is also a new moon, so three sets of offerings fall on the same day.
b: This verse shows how the calendar layers: the daily offering, the new moon offering, and the festival offering are all made on this day. The rabbis drew a rule from such verses: "what is more frequent comes first" (Bavli Zevachim 89a). The seventh month is the busiest of the year, with the day of loud blasts, the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Booths, just as seven is the Bible's number of completeness.

a: You are to humble yourselves
p: The Hebrew is "you will afflict your souls." Jewish tradition has always understood it as fasting.
b: Inniytem et-nafshoteikhem (KJV "afflict your souls") appears in Leviticus 16:29, 31 and 23:27–32. Nefesh often means the throat or appetite, and Psalm 35:13 and Isaiah 58:3–5 link this "humbling" with fasting. The Mishnah lists five things given up on the Day of Atonement: eating and drinking, washing, anointing, sandals, and marital relations (Yoma 8:1). Acts 27:9 calls the day simply "the Fast." The same verb is used for denying oneself in vows (30:13).

a: the sin offering of atonement
p: The special rites of the Day of Atonement are in Leviticus 16. This list gives only the added public offerings.
b: "The sin offering of atonement" refers to the bull and goat whose blood the high priest took into the Most Holy Place (Leviticus 16:11–19). The extra goat here is a separate offering. Hebrews 9:6–14 reads the high priest's yearly entrance as a picture of Christ entering "once for all" with his own blood. In Judaism, after the temple fell, the day became one of prayer, confession and fasting, with the service of the high priest recited in the synagogue.

a: Keep a feast to the LORD for seven days
p: Sukkot, the autumn harvest feast, was the most joyful festival of the year. Israel lived in huts for seven days.
b: Leviticus 23:39–43 tells Israel to live in booths (sukkot) to remember the wilderness. Called simply "the feast" (1 Kings 8:2), it was the great pilgrimage of the year. In the Second Temple, water was poured on the altar and great lamps were lit, and the Mishnah says, "Whoever has not seen the joy of the water-drawing has never seen joy in his life" (Sukkah 5:1). John 7:2, 37–38 places Jesus' call, "Let anyone who is thirsty come to me," on the last great day of this feast. Zechariah 14:16 foresees the nations coming to keep it.
r: Leviticus 23:33–43; Deuteronomy 16:13–15; Nehemiah 8:14–18; Zechariah 14:16–19; John 7:2; John 7:37–39

a: thirteen young bulls
