p: The bulls count down from thirteen to seven: seventy in all. The rabbis said they were offered for the nations.
b: Over the seven days, 13 + 12 + 11 + 10 + 9 + 8 + 7 = 70 bulls. The rabbis connected seventy with the seventy nations of Genesis 10 and said Israel offered them on behalf of the whole world: "Woe to the nations, for they have lost and do not know what they have lost. While the temple stood, the altar atoned for them" (Bavli Sukkah 55b). The single bull of the eighth day stood for Israel alone. Others see the falling numbers as a sign of joy slowly ending. The total of seven times two rams and seven times fourteen lambs keeps sevens throughout.

a: following the rule
p: This short phrase points back to the amounts listed in 28:12–14 and 15:1–12.
b: The phrase ka-mishpat saves repeating the full grain and wine amounts each day. In the Hebrew of 29:18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33 and 37 there are small spelling differences between the days: an extra letter appears in the words for "their drink offerings" on day two (29:19), "its drink offerings" on day six (29:31), and "by their rule" on day seven (29:33). The rabbis noticed that the extra letters, mem, yod and mem, spell mayim, "water," and took this as a hint in the Torah of the water-pouring at the feast (Bavli Taanit 2b–3a).

a: you will have a closing assembly
p: The eighth day is a separate holiday, the "closing assembly." Later it became Simchat Torah.
b: Atseret means a solemn gathering or closing. The eighth day after the seven of Booths has only one bull, one ram and seven lambs, like the day of loud blasts. Rashi compares it to a king who invites all his children to a seven-day feast and then says, "Your leaving is hard for me; stay one more day" with just the family. In later Judaism this is Shemini Atzeret, and in many places the day of Simchat Torah, when the yearly reading of the Torah ends and begins again. John 7:37 may mean this day or the seventh.

a: besides your vow offerings and your freewill offerings
p: The public calendar does not replace the offerings each person brings for vows or out of free will.
b: Vow offerings are brought to fulfill a promise made to God; freewill offerings are given simply from a willing heart (Leviticus 22:18–23; Deuteronomy 12:6). This verse leads into chapter 30, which is about vows. In Hebrew Bibles, 29:40 is 30:1, so chapter 30 begins one verse later in English.

a: the heads of the tribes
t: A law for the tribal heads
p: Unusually, this law is given to the tribal heads. The rabbis took that to mean that experts may release vows.
b: Most laws are spoken to "the Israelites." This one goes to "the heads of the tribes." The Talmud read this as the basis for the rule that a sage, or a court of three ordinary people, can release a person from a vow that should not have been made (Bavli Nedarim 78a). The Mishnah says "the release of vows floats in the air with nothing to rest on," since the Torah barely mentions it (Chagigah 1:8). This later practice is the background of Kol Nidre, the annulment of vows chanted on the eve of the Day of Atonement.

a: When a man makes a vow to the LORD
p: A neder is a promise to give or do something for God; an issar is a pledge to give something up.
b: Two kinds of promise are named. A neder (vow) commits something to God, often on a condition, as when Jacob vowed a tenth if God brought him home (Genesis 28:20–22) or Hannah vowed her son (1 Samuel 1:11). An issar, "bond, pledge," binds oneself to refrain from something, like fasting (30:13). Both are voluntary, but once spoken they are binding: "he must not break his word." Ecclesiastes 5:5 says it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Jephthah's vow (Judges 11:30–40) shows how badly a rash vow could go.
r: Genesis 28:20–22; 1 Samuel 1:11; Judges 11:30–40; Deuteronomy 23:21–23; Ecclesiastes 5:4–5; Psalm 15:4

a: Everything his mouth has spoken, he must do
p: Jesus teaches, "Do not swear at all," and James repeats it. Christians have read this in different ways.
b: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says, "You have heard that it was said to the people of old, 'Do not swear falsely, but keep your oaths to the Lord.' But I tell you not to swear at all ... Let your word be 'Yes, yes' or 'No, no'" (Matthew 5:33–37; compare James 5:12). Quakers, Mennonites and some other groups refuse all oaths. Most churches, following Augustine and the Reformers, hold that Jesus forbids careless and deceitful oaths, not solemn vows and court oaths, since Paul himself took a vow (Acts 18:18) and called God as witness (2 Corinthians 1:23). Jesus' charge against using "corban" vows to avoid caring for parents also draws on vow law (Mark 7:9–13).
r: Matthew 5:33–37; James 5:12; Acts 18:18; Acts 21:23–26; Mark 7:9–13; 2 Corinthians 1:23

a: while she is young and in her father's house
p: The law lets a father or husband cancel a woman's vow. Readers differ sharply on how to judge this.
b: A man's vow stands on its own (30:2), but an unmarried daughter's vow can be canceled by her father, and a wife's by her husband, if he speaks up on the day he hears. A widow or divorced woman's vow stands like a man's (30:9). Many interpreters see a household law protecting the family's property and the husband's or father's responsibility, since a vow often meant giving away goods or giving up marital relations. Feminist readers point out that it treats women's religious promises as under male control. Others note what the law does grant: a woman's vow is binding unless he acts at once, and silence counts as consent.

a: the LORD will forgive her
p: The word salach usually means "forgive." Here it means God holds her free of the broken vow.
b: Salach is normally used of God forgiving sin (14:19–20). Here there is no sin on her part; the point is that God will not hold her guilty for not keeping a vow that was canceled. Some translations therefore say "release" or "absolve." The guilt, if any, falls on the man who canceled it late (30:15).

a: a rash promise from her lips
p: Mivta means a thoughtless word blurted out. The Torah elsewhere requires atonement for rash oaths.
b: The rare word mivta comes from a verb for speaking rashly (Leviticus 5:4; Psalm 106:33, of Moses at Meribah; Proverbs 12:18). Leviticus 5:4–6 requires a guilt offering for one who swears rashly and later realizes it. This verse covers a woman who brings an earlier vow into her marriage: the new husband may cancel it on the day he hears.

a: A widow or a divorced woman is held to her vow
p: A widow or divorced woman has no father or husband over her vow. Her word stands like a man's.
b: This verse shows that the law is about the household, not about women's ability: a woman who heads her own household makes binding vows just as a man does. Widows and divorced women in ancient Israel often had to manage their own property and affairs, and the Bible repeatedly commands care for widows (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 24:17). A divorced woman could, for example, take a Nazirite vow, which Numbers 6 allows to "a man or a woman."

a: any sworn pledge to humble herself
p: "To humble herself" is the same phrase used for fasting on the Day of Atonement (29:7).
b: Le-annot nafesh, "to afflict the soul," usually means fasting or other abstinence (see 29:7). The rabbis said a husband may cancel only vows of self-denial or those that affect the marriage, not every vow (Mishnah Nedarim 11:1). The phrase suggests the common kind of vow in daily life: promises to fast or to give up some food or pleasure.

a: then he will carry her guilt
p: If a husband cancels a vow too late and she obeys him, the guilt for the broken vow is his.
b: A husband who stays silent on the day he hears has confirmed the vow. If he later forbids it, she is caught between God and her husband. The law settles it: he, not she, carries the guilt. Interpreters see here both the limits on the husband's power, which must be used at once and openly, and the law's concern that a woman not be punished for what she could not control.

a: Avenge the Israelites on the Midianites
p: Neqamah in the Bible is usually punishment carried out by a rightful authority, not private revenge.
b: The root naqam covers vengeance, punishment and vindication. In 31:2 it is "the Israelites' vengeance"; in 31:3 Moses calls it "the LORD's vengeance." The Bible forbids private revenge (Leviticus 19:18) and says "vengeance belongs to me" (Deuteronomy 32:35, quoted in Romans 12:19). Here the war is presented as God's judgment for Peor (25:16–18), carried out under his command. That framing is exactly what makes the chapter hard for modern readers. It is also Moses' last act before his death.

a: twelve thousand men equipped for war
p: Twelve thousand men defeat all Midian and lose not one man (31:49). Readers take this as miracle or as ideal story.
b: The force is small, a thousand from each tribe, and it returns with huge spoil and no losses (31:49). Traditional readers see God fighting for Israel, as at Jericho. Many critical scholars, following Martin Noth, think the chapter is a late priestly composition, a kind of model war used to teach rules about purity and the division of spoil, rather than a record of a battle. They point to the round and enormous numbers (675,000 sheep and goats, 32,000 girls) and to the fact that Midian appears again as a strong nation in Judges 6–8.

a: Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest
p: The priest leads, not a general. The war is treated as a holy act, with holy objects and trumpets.
b: Phinehas, the zealot of Peor (25:7–13), now goes with the army. Deuteronomy 20:2–4 says a priest is to address the troops before battle. "The holy articles" may be the ark, as in 10:35 and Joshua 6, or the Urim, or sacred trumpets; the rabbis debated which (Sifre; Rashi). The trumpets for alarm are the silver trumpets of 10:9: "when you go to war ... you will be remembered before the LORD." No Joshua is mentioned, which some see as a sign the chapter is a priestly ideal.

a: they killed every male
p: "Every male" means the fighting men, since boys are killed only later (31:17). Midian survives in later history.
b: Deuteronomy 20:13–14 describes the rule for distant cities: the men are killed, women and children taken. That is what happens here at first. Only after Moses' order (31:15–17) are the boys and most women killed. Midian is not wiped out: in Judges 6–8 Midianite raiders oppress Israel for seven years. Some scholars take "every male" as typical war-report exaggeration, like the claims in the Moabite Mesha stone that "Israel has utterly perished forever."

a: the five kings of Midian
p: Joshua 13:21 names the same five as leaders allied with Sihon, the Amorite king.
b: Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba are called "kings" here and "the leaders of Midian... the princes of Sihon" in Joshua 13:21. Zur was Cozbi's father (25:15). Rekem is also an old name for Petra, the later Nabataean city in Edom (Josephus, Antiquities 4.161), and some think it was a Midianite center. Midian seems to have been a federation of clans, each with its own chief, rather than one kingdom.

a: Balaam son of Beor they also killed with the sword
p: The seer who wanted to die the death of the upright (23:10) dies by the sword among Israel's enemies.
b: Joshua 13:22 adds that Israel killed "Balaam son of Beor, the diviner." Why was he in Midian? The rabbis said he came back to collect his wages for the advice of Peor (Bavli Sanhedrin 106a). The Talmud also says he was 33 years old when he died, citing Psalm 55:23, "Men of blood and deceit / will not reach half their days." His death answers his own prayer in 23:10, ironically. Josephus places Balaam's advice in a long speech to Balak (Antiquities 4.126–130).

a: Every town where they had lived
p: Midian had both towns and tirot, circular camps of tents or stone enclosures.
b: Tirot are encampments, perhaps stone-walled enclosures for herds and tents, used by semi-nomads (Genesis 25:16, of Ishmael's tribes; Psalm 69:25). Archaeologists working in the Hejaz of northwest Arabia, the Midian region, have found settlements and a distinctive painted pottery ("Qurayyah ware") dating to roughly 1300–1100 BC, which some link with the Midianites. The burning is typical of ancient war reports.

a: Moses was furious with the army's officers
p: The officers followed the usual rule of war. Moses is angry because the women of Peor are alive.
b: The army had done what Deuteronomy 20:14 permits: kill the men and keep women, children and animals as spoil. Moses' anger comes from 25:1–18: the women had led Israel into the sin that killed 24,000. The text presents his order as punishment for Peor rather than a general rule of war. Many readers find his anger the hardest moment in the chapter, and the text gives no word of protest from anyone.

a: on Balaam's advice
p: Only here does the Torah blame Balaam for Peor. The New Testament builds on this verse.
b: Chapters 22–24 show Balaam blessing Israel and going home. This verse says that he later gave the advice that led Israel to sin at Peor. Jewish tradition filled in the advice: he told Balak that Israel's God hates sexual sin, so tempt them with women (Josephus, Antiquities 4.126–130; Bavli Sanhedrin 106a). Revelation 2:14 says he "taught Balak to set a trap in front of the Israelites, so that they would eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual sin." 2 Peter 2:15 and Jude 11 add greed. So the later picture of Balaam as the model false teacher rests on this one verse.

a: So now, kill every boy among the little ones
t: The killing of boys and women
p: Moses orders the killing of all boys and all women who are not virgins. Readers have answered this very differently.
b: One of the hardest commands in the Bible, read in three main ways. Defending: a unique judgment on a people that set out to destroy Israel's faith (25:18), with the boys killed so Midian could not rise again (Augustine, Against Faustus 22; Calvin; Paul Copan). Defenders add the text's own reason: the women killed are those who could have taken part at Peor (31:16), and virginity was a rough test of who had not; the Talmud tells how the girls were tested before the high priest's gold plate (Bavli Yevamot 60b). Limiting: the rabbis restricted holy war to the seven nations and Amalek, and Maimonides required an offer of peace first. Eric Seibert and Gregory Boyd argue that God is fully shown in the nonviolent Jesus, so this picture belongs to an earlier stage. Criticizing: John J. Collins and Susan Niditch read it as ideological violence to be judged, not followed. See the chapter page.

a: keep alive for yourselves
p: The girls were taken as captives. The text does not say they were wives, servants or slaves, and readers differ.
b: "Keep alive for yourselves" could mean as servants or as future wives. Deuteronomy 21:10–14 gives a law for marrying a captive woman: she mourns her parents for a month and may not be sold as a slave if later sent away. The rabbis took 31:18 together with that law, and the Talmud uses this verse in discussing whether a priest may marry a convert who came to Israel as a young girl (Bavli Yevamot 60b). Critics say plainly what the words imply: the girls were war captives taken "for yourselves," and sexual use is assumed, as in the captive-bride law of Deuteronomy 21:10–14 (Susan Niditch, War in the Hebrew Bible). The girls had no choice in any of this, and 32 of them went to Eleazar the priest as the LORD's share (31:40–41) and 320 to the Levites (31:30, 47). The text does not suggest they were sacrificed; "the LORD's tax" of people went to the priests as servants.

a: stay outside the camp for seven days
p: Killing in war, even a war God ordered, makes a soldier unclean. He must be purified with the ashes of the red cow.
b: Contact with a corpse makes a person unclean for seven days, and the cure is the water mixed with the ashes of the red cow (19:11–22). That law now applies to soldiers. The Bible elsewhere hints at the cost of shedding blood even in just war: David may not build the temple because he "shed much blood" (1 Chronicles 22:8). Many readers find it significant that the chapter, for all its violence, insists that killing defiles.

a: tin and lead
p: The list of metals matches what ancient metalworkers used, and suits Midian's link with copper mining.
b: Gold, silver, bronze, iron, tin and lead were the six metals known in the ancient Near East. The copper mines at Timna in the Arabah were worked in the 1200s–1100s BC, and Midianite pottery and a small tent shrine with a copper snake were found there, which some scholars connect with the Midianites and with Moses' bronze snake (21:9). Metal objects that can bear fire are purified by fire and water; others by water alone. This is the origin of the Jewish practice of making cookware kosher by fire or boiling (Mishnah Avodah Zarah 5:12).

a: the water for impurity
p: The "water of niddah" is the cleansing water made with the red cow's ashes (19:9).
b: Mei niddah is literally "water of impurity," meaning water that removes impurity (19:9, 13, 20–21). The word niddah is also used for menstrual impurity. Hebrews 9:13–14 mentions "the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are unclean" and contrasts it with the cleansing by Christ's blood.

a: Split the spoil in two
p: Half goes to the fighters, half to the whole people. David makes a similar rule in 1 Samuel 30.
b: The fighters (12,000) receive half; the rest of Israel receives half. A tax goes to God from each: 1 in 500 from the soldiers' half to the priest, 1 in 50 from the people's half to the Levites. David later rules that those who guarded the baggage share equally with those who fought (1 Samuel 30:24–25), "and it became a rule for Israel." The careful sums in 31:32–47 show the law in action.

a: 675,000 sheep and goats
p: The spoil is enormous and the figures divide too neatly. Many scholars think they are ideal numbers.
b: 675,000 + 72,000 + 61,000 animals and 32,000 girls: the totals halve exactly and the taxes come out as whole numbers. Traditional readers take this as a record of a rich nomad people. Others suggest the Hebrew numbers have been inflated, as with the census (see 26:7). Many critical scholars read the list as a model calculation, designed to teach the rule of 1 in 500 and 1 in 50. The figure of 32,000 girls, if literal, implies a total Midianite population of perhaps 100,000 or more killed, which many readers find impossible to square with Judges 6.

a: not one man of ours is missing
p: Twelve thousand fighters return without a loss. The officers respond with an offering.
b: The claim is meant to show God's protection (compare Psalm 91:7). The officers count their men, perhaps remembering that a census needed a ransom "so that no plague will strike them" (Exodus 30:12), and they bring gold as atonement. Critical scholars see the detail as part of the chapter's ideal character. The rabbis said the gold atoned for the soldiers' looking at the captive women with desire (Bavli Shabbat 64a).

a: Let it make atonement for our lives before the LORD
p: "To make atonement" here may mean a ransom for lives, as the census half-shekel was.
b: Le-khapper al nafshoteinu, "to make atonement for our lives," means something close to a ransom here. It echoes Exodus 30:12–16, where every man counted pays half a shekel "as a ransom for his life." The soldiers have just been counted, and they bring a ransom. The 16,750 shekels (about 420 pounds of gold) are placed in the tent of meeting "as a reminder," like the census silver in Exodus 30:16.

a: the land of Jazer and the land of Gilead
p: Gilead is the hill country east of the Jordan, famous for its pastures and its balm.
b: Jazer lay north of Heshbon, and Gilead was the wooded, well-watered highland between the Arnon and the Yarmuk rivers. "Is there no balm in Gilead?" (Jeremiah 8:22) recalls its medicine trade, and the Song of Songs compares hair to "a flock of goats coming down from Mount Gilead" (Song of Songs 4:1). For herders it was ideal. Genesis 31 tells how Jacob and Laban made a covenant here.
r: 21:32; Genesis 31:21–25; Genesis 37:25; Jeremiah 8:22; Song of Songs 4:1

a: Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo and Beon
t: The towns in the Mesha stone
p: Several of these towns appear in the Moabite king Mesha's inscription of about 840 BC.
b: The Mesha stone (the Moabite Stone), found at Dibon in 1868, records King Mesha's revolt against Israel (compare 2 Kings 3:4–27). Mesha writes that "the men of Gad had lived in the land of Ataroth from of old, and the king of Israel built Ataroth for himself," and that he built Baal-meon and captured Nebo. So the Bible's claim that Gad lived around Ataroth is confirmed by an enemy king, though by Mesha's time the land had passed back and forth. "Beon" is a shortened form of Baal-meon (32:38).

a: Why would you turn the hearts of the Israelites away
p: The verb heni means to frustrate or break down. The same root gives God's "opposition" in 14:34.
b: Heni means to hinder or forbid, as a father "forbids" a vow (30:5, 8, 11 use the same verb). The written text and the reading tradition differ slightly in spelling here (Ketiv and Qere), with no change in meaning. In 14:34 God says the people will "know my opposition" (the noun from the same root). Moses fears that two tribes settling early will break the others' will to fight, as the ten spies did.

a: when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea to see the land
p: Moses retells chapters 13–14 as a warning. Deuteronomy 1 retells it again.
b: The retelling shows how the story of the spies became the defining failure of the wilderness generation. Moses calls these men "a new crop of sinners" in their fathers' place (32:14), the same failure in a new form. Deuteronomy 1:19–46 and Psalm 95:8–11 return to it, and Hebrews 3:7–4:11 uses it to warn Christians not to harden their hearts "today." The Valley of Eshcol ("cluster") is where the spies cut the great bunch of grapes (13:23–24).

a: Caleb son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite
p: Only here and in Joshua is Caleb called a Kenizzite, a clan linked with Edom.
b: Kenaz is named among the chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:11, 15, 42), and "the Kenizzites" are a people of Canaan in Genesis 15:19. Calling Caleb a Kenizzite suggests his clan had joined Judah from outside, as other groups did. Joshua 14:6–14 and 15:13–19 tell how he received Hebron. Caleb thus stands as an example of an outsider who "followed the LORD fully," alongside Joshua.

a: He kept them wandering in the wilderness for forty years
p: The verb means to make someone stagger or wander aimlessly. The forty years were a punishment.
b: Va-yeni'em is from nua, "to shake, stagger, wander," used of Cain the wanderer (Genesis 4:12) and drunks reeling (Isaiah 24:20). The forty years in 14:33–34 match the forty days of spying, a year for a day. Some writers have pictured the forty years as constant travel; the itinerary in chapter 33 and Deuteronomy 1:46 suggest much of the time was spent at Kadesh.

a: We will build sheep pens here for our livestock, and towns for our little ones
p: The tribes mention their sheep before their children. Moses' answer reverses the order (32:24).
b: Rashi noticed that the tribes said "pens for our livestock, and towns for our little ones," putting property first, and that Moses answered "build towns for your little ones and pens for your flocks" (32:24), correcting the order. The Midrash says they loved their money more than their children, and that is why the eastern tribes were the first to go into exile (Numbers Rabbah 22; compare 1 Chronicles 5:26). Other readers see only a natural way of speaking. The plan itself is fair: the fighting men will cross first.

a: You will be free of guilt toward the LORD and toward Israel
p: The phrase became a Jewish principle: one must be clear in the eyes of people, not only before God.
b: Neqiyyim me-YHWH u-mi-Yisra'el, "clean before the LORD and before Israel." The Mishnah uses it to teach that officials handling public money should avoid even the appearance of wrongdoing, "for a person must be clear before people just as before God" (Mishnah Shekalim 3:2). Paul says something similar: "we plan what is right, not only before the Lord but also before people" (2 Corinthians 8:21).

a: Know this: your sin will find you
p: A famous saying. In context, "sin" may also mean the punishment that sin brings.
b: The KJV "be sure your sin will find you out" became a proverb about hidden sins being discovered. In context, Moses is not talking about secret sins but about breaking a public promise. Chatta't can mean both sin and its consequence (compare Genesis 4:7, sin "crouching at the door"). Moses warns that their failure would come back on them as punishment. The saying works in both senses.
orig: וּדְעוּ חַטַּאתְכֶם אֲשֶׁר תִּמְצָא אֶתְכֶם (ude'u chatta'tkhem asher timtsa etkhem)

a: the half-tribe of Manasseh son of Joseph
p: Half of Manasseh appears suddenly at the end, without having asked for land.
b: Only Gad and Reuben made the request (32:1–5). Yet Moses gives land to half of Manasseh as well, and 32:39–42 tells how Machir, Jair and Nobah captured parts of Gilead and Bashan. Critical scholars see two traditions joined. Traditional readers suppose part of Manasseh joined the request, or that their conquests in the north earned them land. Joshua 22 tells of the eastern tribes' altar by the Jordan and the fear that the river would divide Israel.

a: their names were changed
p: Nebo and Baal-meon were named after gods. The Israelites gave them other names.
b: Nebo was a Babylonian and Moabite god (Isaiah 46:1), and Baal-meon includes the name of Baal. The parenthesis may be a scribe's note telling readers not to pronounce these names, in line with Exodus 23:13, "Do not even mention the names of other gods." Rashi said the Amorites had named the towns after their idols, so the Reubenites renamed them. The old names survived anyway, as the Mesha stone shows.

a: called them Havvoth-jair
p: Chavvot means tent camps or villages. Judges 10:3–4 tells of a later Jair with thirty towns.
b: Chavvot is related to an Arabic word for a circle of tents. Deuteronomy 3:14 places them in Bashan; 1 Kings 4:13 and 1 Chronicles 2:22–23 mention them in Gilead. Judges 10:3–4 tells of Jair the judge, whose thirty sons rode thirty donkeys and had thirty towns "called Havvoth-jair to this day." Many scholars think the place name drew more than one story to itself.

a: Moses wrote down the places they set out from
p: One of the few places where the Torah says Moses wrote something down. What exactly did he write?
b: The Torah says Moses wrote the war record against Amalek (Exodus 17:14), "the scroll of the covenant" (Exodus 24:4–7), the words of Exodus 34:27, this itinerary, and "this teaching" (Deuteronomy 31:9, 24). Traditional Jewish and Christian readers have taken such notes as evidence that Moses wrote the Torah. Critical scholars see these as the few things tradition credited to him, which later grew into the claim that he wrote it all. Notice the order: "starting points, stage by stage," then "stages, by their starting points." Ancient readers loved such reversals; modern ones see a mirror pattern (chiasm).

a: with a hand raised high
p: The itinerary begins with a short summary of the exodus, using the words of Exodus 12 and 14.
b: "On the day after the Passover" and "with a hand raised high" echo Exodus 14:8, and the burial of the firstborn recalls Exodus 12:29–30. "Judgments on their gods" repeats Exodus 12:12. A raised hand is a gesture of victory or defiance. The summary reminds the new generation at the Jordan where the journey began.

a: On their gods, too, the LORD had carried out judgments
p: How did God judge Egypt's gods? Readers point to the plagues, or to the idols' destruction.
b: Exodus 12:12 promised it, and this verse says it happened. Many readers since Philo and the rabbis have seen each plague as aimed at an Egyptian god: the Nile, frogs (Heqet), cattle (Hathor, Apis), the sun (Ra). Some scholars accept parts of this; others think it reads too much into the plagues. The rabbis said idols of wood rotted and those of metal melted (Mekhilta; Rashi on Exodus 12:12). Either way the point is that Israel's God showed himself greater than all the powers of Egypt.

a: camped at Succoth
p: From Rameses to the plains of Moab, the list names forty-two camps. About half appear nowhere else.
b: Counting each stop gives 42 camps (or 40 journeys, depending on how one counts). Many names in 33:18–35 are unknown elsewhere. The route roughly matches Exodus and Numbers but does not mention Kibroth-hattaavah's quails, the spies or the rebellions; it is a bare list. Graham Davies compared it with other ancient itineraries. Charles Krahmalkov argued that the stages of 33:44–50 (Iyim, Dibon, Abel) match a route listed in Egyptian topographical lists of the 1400s–1200s BC; others find the evidence weak. Critical scholars often think the list was drawn up later from known stations.

a: crossed through the middle of the sea
p: The crossing of the sea is named in a few words, as one stage among many.
b: Exodus 14–15 tells the crossing at length. Here it is one clause. "Into the wilderness" is the Wilderness of Etham, called "Shur" in Exodus 15:22. Paul calls the crossing a kind of baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–2). On where the sea was, see the topic on the Sea of Reeds.

a: camped by the Sea of Reeds
p: After Elim the people camp by the Sea of Reeds again. Exodus does not mention this stop.
b: This verse shows that Yam Suf can mean the Gulf of Suez or the Red Sea in general, since the route goes south along the coast of Sinai after the crossing (compare 1 Kings 9:26, where Yam Suf is the Gulf of Aqaba). That makes the name harder to pin to one place. Exodus 16:1 goes straight from Elim to the Wilderness of Sin.

a: There was no water there for the people to drink
p: The list stops to recall the thirst at Rephidim (Exodus 17:1–7).
b: At Rephidim God gave water from the rock and Israel fought Amalek (Exodus 17). The itinerary's rare comments (Elim's springs, Rephidim's thirst, Aaron's death) give a few landmarks in a long list. The note on water may also connect with the second water story at Kadesh (20:2–13).

a: Bene-jaakan
p: Deuteronomy 10:6–7 gives some of these stations in a different order and places Aaron's death at Moserah.
b: Here the order is Moseroth, Bene-jaakan, Hor-haggidgad, Jotbathah. Deuteronomy 10:6–7 has Beeroth Bene-jaakan, Moserah (where "Aaron died and was buried"), Gudgodah, Jotbathah. But Numbers 20:22–29 and 33:38 say Aaron died on Mount Hor. Traditional readers explain that Moserah was the district around Mount Hor, or that Israel passed some stations twice. Critical scholars see two traditions about the route and about Aaron's death.

a: Ezion-geber
p: Ezion-geber was a port at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, later Solomon's harbor (1 Kings 9:26).
b: It is usually placed near modern Eilat and Aqaba, perhaps at Tell el-Kheleifeh. Its presence in the list means the route went down to the Gulf of Aqaba and back up to Kadesh. Excavations at Tell el-Kheleifeh found remains from the 700s BC and later, not earlier, which critical scholars use to argue the itinerary reflects later geography. Others suggest the early port lay elsewhere nearby.

a: It was the first day of the fifth month
t: The only dated death in the Torah
p: Aaron's death is the only death in the Torah given an exact date: the first of Av, in the fortieth year.
b: The date became important in Jewish memory. The month of Av also holds the ninth of Av (Tisha b'Av), the fast for the destruction of both temples. Jewish tradition counts the first of Av as Aaron's memorial day (yahrzeit). Aaron's age, 123, matches Exodus 7:7, where he is 83 at the start of the exodus. The rabbis saw Aaron as the lover of peace: "Be disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace" (Mishnah Avot 1:12).

a: the king of Arad, a Canaanite
p: The verse repeats 21:1. Arad in the Negev had an Israelite fortress and temple in the period of the kings.
b: The note recalls Israel's battle with the king of Arad (21:1–3). Excavations at Tel Arad found an Early Bronze Age city and, on a nearby hill, an Iron Age Israelite fortress with a small temple and two standing stones. But there are no remains from the Late Bronze Age, the usual date for the exodus, which is one of the archaeological puzzles of this period. Some scholars suggest the Canaanite Arad was at a different site, such as Tel Malhata.

a: their carved stone figures
p: Maskiyyot are carved stones or figured slabs. Bamot are high places, open-air shrines.
b: Maskit (Leviticus 26:1, "carved stone") is an image or decorated stone. "Images of cast metal" are like the golden calf (Exodus 32:4). The bamot, "high places," were raised shrines, often on hills, and later the books of Kings judge each king by whether he removed them (1 Kings 15:14; 2 Kings 18:4). The command looks ahead to Deuteronomy 7:5 and 12:2–3.
r: Leviticus 26:1; Exodus 23:24; Exodus 34:13; Deuteronomy 7:5; Deuteronomy 12:2–3; 2 Kings 18:4

a: barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides
p: The image returns in Joshua and Judges, and lies behind the English idiom "a thorn in the side."
b: Joshua warns that if Israel mixes with the remaining peoples they will be "a lash on your sides and thorns in your eyes" (Joshua 23:13), and Judges 2:3 repeats it after Israel fails to drive them out. Paul's "thorn in the flesh" (2 Corinthians 12:7) uses a different word but a similar picture. The judges period shows the warning coming true.

a: what I planned to do to them, I will do to you
p: The command to drive out the land's people raises moral questions. Israel is warned the same fate could fall on it.
b: The verb here is "drive out" (horish), not "destroy" (compare the ban of Deuteronomy 7:2; 20:16–17). The last verse turns the warning on Israel: if it copies the land's peoples, it will be driven out too, which the Bible says later happened in the exiles (Leviticus 18:24–28; 2 Kings 17). Readers differ on how to understand the conquest: as God's judgment on the sins of Canaan (Genesis 15:16), as idealized national memory with little basis in history (most archaeologists), or as a text whose violence must be faced honestly. See the topic on holy war.

a: the land of Canaan with these borders
p: The Bible gives several descriptions of the promised land. This one is the land of Canaan west of the Jordan.
b: Genesis 15:18 promises Abram the land "from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates." This chapter draws a smaller map: Canaan from the Wilderness of Zin to Lebo-hamath, the Mediterranean to the Jordan. Many scholars note that it matches the Egyptian province of Canaan in the late 1200s BC, as known from Egyptian texts. Ezekiel 47:13–20 gives nearly the same borders for the restored land. The land east of the Jordan is not included; it is an extra (32; 34:13–15).
r: Genesis 15:18–21; Exodus 23:31; Deuteronomy 1:7; Joshua 15:1–12; Ezekiel 47:13–20; 1 Kings 8:65

a: the tip of the Salt Sea
p: The Bible's name for the Dead Sea, the lowest place on the earth's land surface.
b: The "Salt Sea" (Yam ha-Melach) lies about 1,400 feet below sea level and is so salty that no fish live in it. The name "Dead Sea" comes from Greek and Latin writers. Ezekiel 47:8–10 pictures a river from the temple making its water fresh, with fishermen along its shore.

a: the Scorpion Pass
p: Ma'aleh Akrabbim, "the ascent of scorpions," is a steep pass in the Negev southwest of the Dead Sea.
b: The pass is usually identified with Naqb es-Safa, a climb on the road from the Arabah up toward Mamshit. Kadesh-barnea, the camp where Israel spent many years, is generally placed at Ein el-Qudeirat in northeastern Sinai. Hazar-addar and Azmon are not certainly located. Joshua 15:1–4 gives the same southern border for Judah.

a: the Wadi of Egypt
p: The "Wadi of Egypt" is a dry streambed in northern Sinai, usually identified with Wadi el-Arish.
b: This border is not the Nile. The nachal Mitsrayim is a seasonal stream that marks the edge of Egypt's sphere of control. Assyrian kings also mention it as the border of Egypt. Genesis 15:18 uses a different phrase, "the river (nahar) of Egypt," which some take as the Nile, others as the same wadi.

a: the Great Sea
p: The Bible's "Great Sea" is the Mediterranean. Israel seldom held its coast.
b: In practice Israel rarely controlled the coastal plain; the Philistines held the south and the Phoenicians the north. The border is the ideal, not what Israel usually held. Joshua 13:2–6 lists the land that "remains" to be taken.

a: Lebo-hamath
t: "The entrance of Hamath" or a town?
p: Older versions read "the entrance of Hamath." Most scholars now read Lebo-hamath as a town, modern Lebweh.
b: The KJV reads "the entrance of Hamath" (levo, "to come"). Many scholars identify Lebo as Lebweh in the northern Beqaa Valley of Lebanon, named in Egyptian and Assyrian sources. It was the northern limit of Solomon's kingdom (1 Kings 8:65) and of Jeroboam II's (2 Kings 14:25). "Mount Hor" in 34:7 is not the Mount Hor where Aaron died; it is an unknown peak in the north, perhaps in the Lebanon range.

a: the Sea of Chinnereth
p: Chinnereth (Hebrew Kinneret) is the Old Testament name for the Sea of Galilee, perhaps from kinnor, "lyre," for its shape.
b: The lake was later called Gennesaret (Luke 5:1), the Sea of Tiberias (John 21:1), and the Sea of Galilee. A town of Kinnereth stood on its northwest shore. The rabbis explained the name from its harp shape or its sweet fruit. Much of Jesus' ministry took place along this shore.
r: Deuteronomy 3:17; Joshua 12:3; Joshua 13:27; Luke 5:1; John 21:1; Matthew 4:18

a: the nine tribes and the half-tribe
p: Two and a half tribes already have land east of the Jordan, so the west is for nine and a half.
b: Levi has no tribal land (26:62), and Joseph counts as two tribes (Ephraim and Manasseh), so there are still twelve shares in all. Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh received theirs in chapter 32. Joshua 14:1–5 carries out the division west of the Jordan.

a: Eleazar the priest and Joshua son of Nun
p: The priest is named before Joshua. In Joshua 14:1 they divide the land together.
b: The pairing of priest and leader runs through the end of Numbers (27:21; 32:28). Eleazar is named first, as in Joshua 14:1; 19:51; 21:1. The tribal leaders listed in 34:19–28 are all new names, except Caleb, a sign of the new generation. The order of the tribes runs roughly from south to north, as they would later settle, which differs from every other list in Numbers.

a: Caleb son of Jephunneh
p: Caleb is the only tribal leader from the spy story still living. He is still Judah's leader.
b: Of the twelve men sent to spy out the land (13:1–16), only Caleb and Joshua survived (14:38). Caleb represented Judah then (13:6) and represents it again now, forty years later. Joshua 14:10–11 has him say, at 85, "Even today I have the strength I had on the day Moses sent me. I am as strong now as I was then."

a: cities to live in
p: The Levites have no tribal land, so every tribe gives them cities. Joshua 21 lists all forty-eight.
b: Joshua 21 and 1 Chronicles 6:54–81 list the forty-eight cities, four from most tribes. Scholars have debated whether the list reflects Moses' time, the time of David and Solomon (W. F. Albright and Benjamin Mazar dated it to the united monarchy, when royal officials may have been placed in such cities), or a later ideal. Jacob's curse on Simeon and Levi, "I will divide them among Jacob / and spread them thin through Israel" (Genesis 49:7), comes true in a positive way: Levi is scattered to teach Israel (Deuteronomy 33:10).

a: a thousand cubits out from the city wall on every side
t: A thousand cubits or two thousand?
p: The pastureland reaches 1,000 cubits out (35:4) but is measured as 2,000 cubits (35:5). How do these fit?
b: A cubit is about 18 inches, so 1,000 cubits is about 1,500 feet. Several solutions have been offered. In Mishnah Sotah 5:3, Rabbi Akiva said the 1,000 cubits were the pastureland and the 2,000 the Sabbath limit; Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yose the Galilean said 1,000 cubits of pasture and 2,000 of fields and vineyards. Others say 2,000 is the total length of each side of a square around a small town, measured from the center point. Milgrom proposed a square of 2,000 cubits on each side with the town in the middle. Akiva's reading is one source of the limit of a "Sabbath day's journey" (compare Acts 1:12).

a: cities of refuge
p: Among the Levites' cities are six where someone who killed by accident could flee. Joshua 20 names them.
b: Joshua 20:7–8 names them: Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem, and Hebron west of the Jordan; Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead, and Golan to the east. They were spread so that no one was too far from one. Exodus 21:13 had promised "a place for you where he can run for refuge"; earlier, people fled to the altar (Exodus 21:14; 1 Kings 1:50; 2:28). Placing refuge in Levite cities linked it with holy ground.

a: A killer who has struck someone down by mistake
p: The word rotseach means "one who kills," whether by murder or by accident. Context decides.
b: Ratsach is the verb in the Ten Words, "You must not murder" (Exodus 20:13). This chapter shows it can also be used of accidental killing (35:11, 25–28) and even of the lawful execution of a murderer (35:30). So it means killing a human being in a way that brings blood guilt and needs an answer. This translation uses "killer" where the case is open or accidental and "murderer" where it is deliberate (35:16–21). Bi-shgagah, "by mistake," is the same word used for unintentional sins in Leviticus 4 and Numbers 15:22–29.

a: from the avenger
p: The avenger is the go'el, the same word for the family "redeemer" in Ruth and Leviticus.
b: Go'el ha-dam, "redeemer of blood," is the nearest relative, whose duty was to restore what the family had lost: buy back land (Leviticus 25:25), marry a widow (Ruth 3–4), or answer for a murdered relative's blood. Before courts and police, family vengeance was how murder was punished. The law here limits it: the avenger may not kill until the community has judged. Isaiah calls God Israel's Go'el (Isaiah 41:14).

a: for the foreigner and the settler living among them
p: The cities protect not only Israelites but also foreigners living in Israel.
b: The ger (foreigner, resident alien) and the toshav (settler) receive the same protection. Israel's law often says "one law for the native and the foreigner" (15:15–16; Exodus 12:49; Leviticus 24:22). It is a striking equality: a foreigner who kills an Israelite by accident is also safe until judged.

a: with an iron tool
t: How to tell murder from accident
p: The law gives tests: the weapon, the intent, and whether there was hatred or lying in wait.
b: Three weapons are listed (iron, a stone "in the hand," a wooden tool "in the hand") that are capable of killing. The use of such a weapon suggests intent. Then 35:20–23 adds tests of motive: hatred, hostility, lying in wait. Deuteronomy 19:5 gives an example of an accident: an axe head flying off while cutting wood. Ancient laws such as Hammurabi's also distinguished accidental from intentional harm in some cases, though Israel's system of refuge cities is unique.

a: until the high priest dies
p: The killer is free when the high priest dies. Readers have seen in this a kind of atonement.
b: The Talmud says the high priest's death atones for the killing, since blood guilt needs a death (Bavli Makkot 11b), and also that the high priest should have prayed that no such deaths happen in his time. It adds that the high priest's mother used to bring food and clothing to the refugees, so they would not pray for her son's death (Makkot 11a). Others see an amnesty: a new high priest began a new era, like a king's coronation. Christian writers from the church fathers on saw a picture of Christ, whose death sets the guilty free (Hebrews 6:18 speaks of those "who have fled for refuge").

a: the avenger will not be guilty of blood
p: If the refugee leaves the city, the avenger may kill him without guilt. The city is protection, not punishment.
b: "There is no blood for him" means the avenger bears no guilt. The refugee is safe only inside the city's border, and the rabbis said the border included the pastureland of 35:4–5 (Bavli Makkot 12a). Living in the city is a kind of exile, but it is also protection. The rabbis required that the roads to the cities be kept in good repair with signs reading "Refuge, refuge" (Bavli Makkot 10b).

a: only on the word of witnesses
p: No one may be executed on the word of one witness. The rule returns in Deuteronomy and the New Testament.
b: Deuteronomy 17:6 and 19:15 require two or three witnesses for any conviction. The rule protected the accused and was used against false witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:16–21). Jesus refers to it in Matthew 18:16 and John 8:17, Paul in 2 Corinthians 13:1 and 1 Timothy 5:19. The Gospels show it being abused at Jesus' trial, when witnesses did not agree (Mark 14:56–59).
r: Deuteronomy 17:6; Deuteronomy 19:15; Matthew 18:16; John 8:17; 2 Corinthians 13:1; Mark 14:56–59

a: Do not take a ransom for the life of a murderer
p: Many ancient laws let a killer pay the victim's family. Israel's law forbids it for murder.
b: The Hittite laws, for example, let a killer settle by giving persons or payment to the victim's heirs, and blood money was common in many cultures, including later Arabia. The Torah forbids it: a human life cannot be priced, because humans are made in God's image (Genesis 9:6). The only case where ransom is allowed is the goring ox (Exodus 21:30). The rich could not buy their way out of murder.

a: Blood pollutes the land
p: Murder pollutes the land itself, and no atonement can be made for it except by the murderer's death.
b: In the Bible the land is alive to moral evil: Abel's blood cries out from the ground (Genesis 4:10), and the land "vomits out" peoples who defile it (Leviticus 18:25–28). Deuteronomy 21:1–9 provides a rite when the killer is unknown. Unavenged blood was thought to bring drought or famine (2 Samuel 21:1–14). Modern readers have used the verse in debates about the death penalty, both to support it and, among many Jewish and Christian thinkers, to argue that the courts' strict demands show how rarely it should be carried out (Mishnah Makkot 1:10).
r: Genesis 4:10–11; Genesis 9:6; Leviticus 18:25–28; Deuteronomy 21:1–9; 2 Samuel 21:1–14; Psalm 106:38

a: for I, the LORD, live among the Israelites
p: The book's last law ends with God's presence: the land must be kept clean because he lives there.
b: The verb shakhan, "dwell," is the root of mishkan, "tabernacle" (Exodus 25:8; 29:45). The Jewish idea of the Shekhinah, God's dwelling presence, comes from it. John 1:14 uses a Greek word that echoes it: the Word "pitched his tent among us." Holiness is not only for the sanctuary; it reaches the whole land.

a: the family heads of the clan of Gilead's descendants
p: The men of the daughters' clan raise a problem with the ruling of 27:1–11.
b: Chapter 27 settled who inherits. Now Zelophehad's kinsmen ask what happens when an heiress marries. Under Israelite custom, a married woman's property went with her into her husband's family. The land would pass to another tribe. Their concern is the same one the daughters had: keeping a family's land in the family. The book of Numbers, which began with tribes counted and camped in order, ends with the tribes' land kept intact.

a: when the Israelites' Jubilee comes
p: In the Jubilee, sold land goes back to its first owners. But inherited land through marriage would not return.
b: Leviticus 25:10–28 says land sold returns to the original family every fiftieth year. The men argue that inherited land, unlike sold land, would not return, and the Jubilee would actually fix the transfer for good. Interpreters have found the argument hard: Rashi says it means that even the Jubilee would not bring it back. Many scholars think this verse is a later addition. Either way, it is one of the few places outside Leviticus that mentions the Jubilee.

a: The tribe of Joseph's descendants has spoken rightly
p: God says the men are right, just as he said the daughters were right (27:7).
b: The same phrase (ken ... dovrim) was used for the daughters in 27:7. Both claims are accepted, and the law is balanced: daughters inherit, and heiresses marry within the tribe. The rabbis taught that this rule applied only to that generation. The Talmud says that on the fifteenth of Av, the tribes were allowed to marry one another again, and that this became a day of joy (Bavli Taanit 30b; Mishnah Taanit 4:8).

a: Let them marry whoever is good in their eyes
p: The daughters may choose their husbands, but only within their father's tribe.
b: The verse gives the women a choice, which is notable in a world of arranged marriages, but within a limit. Readers differ on the overall picture. Some see the book's last chapter as protecting women's rights won in chapter 27 while keeping the tribal order. Others, including many feminist scholars, see the ending as a step back: the daughters' gain is fenced so that men's land is safe. Both readings take the text seriously. Tobit 6:11–13 and 7:10–13 show that marrying within the family was still valued centuries later.

a: must marry a man from a clan of her father's tribe
p: The book of Tobit builds its love story on this rule.
b: Tobit, a Jewish story from about 200 BC that Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include, is the main early reading of this law. Tobit marries within his family line (Tobit 1:9), and he tells his son to choose a wife from his father's tribe and not an outsider (Tobit 4:12–13). Sarah is an only daughter who will inherit, so Tobias, as her closest kinsman, has the first right to marry her (Tobit 6:12–13). Numbers only says an heiress must marry inside her tribe. Tobit treats it as a duty for every Israelite, and links the law of Moses to the land and the family line kept whole even in exile.

a: became the wives of their uncles' sons
p: The sisters married their cousins, keeping the land in the family and the clan.
b: Marriage between cousins was common in the ancient Near East and is still practiced in parts of the Middle East. Isaac married Rebekah, his father's brother's granddaughter, and Jacob married his uncle Laban's daughters (Genesis 24; 29). The order of the names here differs from 27:1 and 26:33; the Talmud says one list follows their age and the other their wisdom (Bavli Bava Batra 120a). Joshua 17:3–6 records that they received land among their uncles.

a: on the plains of Moab, beside the Jordan across from Jericho
p: Numbers ends where Deuteronomy begins: on the plains of Moab, at the edge of the land.
b: The book opened at Sinai (1:1) and closes on the plains of Moab, using a summary like Leviticus 27:34. Here the old generation is dead, a new one is counted, Joshua is appointed, the land is mapped and its laws are given. Deuteronomy continues in the same place with Moses' last speeches. Dennis Olson called the book's shape "the death of the old and the birth of the new." It ends not with a story but with five women and their land, a hopeful close: Israel's families will have a future in the land.
